cues.why: Emphasizes lack of intact tissue, encouraging a get-more-intact-tissue heuristic toward excision. In combination with the dual-processing choices, however, the largest/more-comprehensive specimen plan becomes a testwise favorite.

cues.phrase: Predominantly nonviable cells; no interpretable clonality result
cues.why: Beside fresh/fixed versus formalin labels, ordinary association of fresh with viable favors both fresh/fixed choices. The observation legitimately identifies an unresolved study, but a fresh label alone does not explain the prior failure or guarantee viability in the next sample. This is a partial cue, not a reason to remove the failed result.

Combines the apparently larger specimen with both processing streams. The balanced matrix prevents majority-component convergence, but does not prevent a choose-more-tissue-and-more-tests shortcut when no competing burden or adequacy tradeoff is evident. This is a weaker comprehensiveness cue than the prior solid-versus-debris giveaway and still requires some familiarity with biopsy terminology.

fairness: One-best-answer: excision with planned histologic and ancillary allocation is a plausible strongest plan for this accessible node after limited same-target sampling. The mobile/superficial anatomy is genuine procedural context, not by itself a gratuitous permission sentence. A well-planned core with appropriate allocation remains a clinically credible competitor. Whether the supplied facts establish a sufficiently strong preference for excision is precisely the held comparison; I cannot certify unique superiority or assert that core is equally good without that verification.

The intended contrast can be inferred from the matrix, but the after labels do not literally make the processing options mutually exclusive. The rationale outside the after fields cannot supply the missing whole-specimen qualifier. This is a concrete fairness repair, not merely a desire for longer labels.

Specimen limitation: the previous flow result establishes failure to obtain an interpretable result, but does not identify why cells were nonviable. The text must not be read as proving that formalin caused that failure or that any fresh allocation will solve it. The significance of EBV in blood or scattered cells likewise does not by itself provide a complete tissue classification. No exact diagnosis or treatment is established here.

Difficulty: moderate, with two meaningful operations: interpret what the prior same-node specimen leaves unanswered, then combine a representative method with handling suited to the remaining studies. Unlike round one, both methods address the solid node, so there are no waste-target foils. The processing ambiguity and unverified method preference are not counted as desirable difficulty. The more-is-better shortcut still lowers discrimination.

Importance/realism: obtaining adequate nodal tissue and coordinating specimen handling are practically important surgical responsibilities and plausible high-yield resident learning. The transplant setting is a credible reason for careful classification. The exact PTLD method preference is more specialized than the general sampling principle and needs hematopathology input. The exhibit is a sampling/laboratory record, not an image-reading task.

Owner flag: fully resolved in the broad requested sense that each answer now specifies a biopsy method and a processing plan rather than generic care coordination. The narrower whole-specimen allocation ambiguity remains a new repair. Specificity does not establish clinical ranking or source adequacy, and this report makes no claim that the candidate is live.

The hold remains open; no universal excision rule or categorical failure of core biopsy is accepted.

packet.title: Reassess a changed blood-cell pattern before another ITP treatment
packet.keyOrderNotice: key shown first for review only; runtime answer choices are randomized
packet.reviewDisplayNote: Jamie Taylor is a review placeholder. Before is the reviewed round-one draft, except G03 and G04-R which bind directly to the flagged live source. The original G04 remains live. Source holds and self-checks do not authorize acceptance.
packet.ownerNote: I thought another version of this question was HIV/HCV first then bone marrow testing second

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 57-year-old woman, is seen for bruising five months after isolated thrombocytopenia was first documented. Platelets rose during corticosteroid treatment and fell again during tapering. Hemoglobin and leukocyte counts remain within laboratory reference ranges; smear review describes normal red-cell and white-cell morphology.
before.Current update: The returned HIV and hepatitis-C serology is negative. Platelet counts since the relapse have remained above 30 × 10^9/L. Bruises have recurred, but there has been no mucosal or internal bleeding. Hematology is continuing treatment and follow-up; Jamie Taylor asks about an operation after the relapse.
before.Task: Which plan should be recommended for Jamie Taylor's splenectomy consultation?
Options: **KEY:** Continue treatment; reassess elective splenectomy when disease duration reaches a year
Arrange vaccination; schedule splenectomy after preoperative immunization is complete
Arrange marrow sampling; schedule splenectomy after the pathology report returns

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 57-year-old woman, is seen five months after isolated thrombocytopenia was documented. Platelets rose during corticosteroid treatment and fell during tapering. At the initial assessment, hemoglobin, neutrophil count and red-cell morphology were within laboratory reference limits.
after.Current update: HIV and hepatitis-C serology have returned negative. At this return visit, hemoglobin and the absolute neutrophil count are below their laboratory reference ranges. The smear describes macrocytic red cells and neutrophils with reduced granulation and fewer nuclear lobes. Vitamin B12 and folate are within reference ranges; the reticulocyte count is below range.
after.Task: Which investigation should precede another treatment recommendation for Jamie Taylor's thrombocytopenia?

before: **KEY:** Continue treatment; reassess elective splenectomy when disease duration reaches a year

This remains an early persistent course. In this nonemergency presentation, ongoing treatment and reassessment are preferable to committing to early elective splenectomy; the recorded ASH claim supports waiting at least a year when possible.
Arrange vaccination; schedule splenectomy after preoperative immunization is complete

Vaccination is relevant when an operation is selected, but completing it does not resolve whether elective splenectomy is appropriate at this early point. This choice turns preparation for surgery into its indication.
Arrange marrow sampling; schedule splenectomy after the pathology report returns

A marrow result would not itself resolve the early elective-surgery timing issue. This is not a claim that marrow evaluation is never appropriate: a separate indication requires its own assessment, and negative HIV/HCV results do not mandate a universal marrow-then-surgery sequence.
after: **KEY:** Marrow aspirate and core biopsy

The initial isolated platelet problem has become a multilineage cytopenia with altered cell morphology. Marrow assessment can examine production, morphology and tissue together before this is treated as another uncomplicated ITP relapse. The indication is the changed pattern, not the negative viral serology.
Peripheral-blood flow cytometry assay

Flow cytometry is a credible investigation of an abnormal blood-cell population. Here the reported changes concern multiple lineages and maturation, and a blood immunophenotype would not supply the marrow morphology and tissue assessment underlying the intended next step. This is not a claim that flow studies have no role in the subsequent workup.
Peripheral-blood myeloid sequencing assay

Molecular testing could contribute to classification, but a detected clone would not by itself establish the tissue/morphologic explanation of this changed cytopenia pattern. The near-miss is substituting a molecular result for the integrated marrow evaluation.

Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; administer prophylactic dantrolene

before: **KEY:** Propofol infusion with remifentanil; rocuronium for intubation

The first-degree family result warrants managing the patient as potentially susceptible until assessed. An uncomplicated previous exposure does not establish absence of susceptibility. This regimen avoids both volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine.
Sevoflurane maintenance with fentanyl; cisatracurium for intubation
This is a familiar anaesthetic regimen and reproduces a drug previously tolerated, but sevoflurane remains an MH trigger. A prior uneventful anaesthetic does not clear the family-history risk.
Propofol infusion with fentanyl; succinylcholine for intubation

Intravenous maintenance can be suitable, but the induction/intubation component also matters: succinylcholine remains a trigger. A plan is not made trigger-free merely by replacing the maintenance agent.
after: **KEY:** Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; arrange contracture testing separately

The uneventful exposure and negative panel do not clear susceptibility in this family. With the represented nontriggering plan and documented MH preparation, definitive susceptibility testing need not become a prerequisite to surgery.
Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; administer prophylactic dantrolene

This retains an appropriate intravenous technique but adds prophylaxis as though familial risk requires pretreatment even with trigger avoidance and MH preparation. It confuses readiness to treat a crisis with routinely administering the rescue drug.
Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia after muscle-contracture testing

The family result and negative panel justify continued risk precautions, not necessarily delaying surgery until a definitive susceptibility test is completed. This is a credible sequencing error when an inconclusive genetic result is treated as a barrier to a nontriggering anesthetic.

before: **KEY:** Targeted breast ultrasound

after: **KEY:** Request targeted breast ultrasound

The complete acquisition record corresponds to the other marker, not the persistent lower-inner finding. Targeted imaging should be correlated with the current palpable site. This requests a different acquisition rather than simply repeating an adequate study.

Retrieval is a credible near-miss when an acquisition exists but transferred images are missing. The complete recorded acquisition here addresses the other marker, so retrieving that accession would not supply the required clinical-site correlation.

This would be reasonable if the mammographic acquisition did not cover the current marker. The supplied views already include it; the unresolved issue is targeted sonographic correlation with the actual clinical finding, not another mammographic view.

before: **KEY:** Serum hCG measurement
The correct answer is “Serum hCG measurement.” Pregnancy status belongs in this evaluation because pregnancy is possible; the result must be interpreted with the clinical findings.
Complete blood count
This does not establish whether the patient is pregnant.
Serum lipase testing
This does not establish whether the patient is pregnant.
Serum creatinine testing
This does not establish whether the patient is pregnant.
after: **KEY:** Transvaginal ultrasonography with gynecologic assessment

The early home result, falling but detectable hCG and transabdominal scan do not establish pregnancy location. The new focal symptoms require prompt assessment of an early-pregnancy complication rather than a conclusion of completed miscarriage or a settled appendiceal diagnosis.
Appendiceal MRI with general-surgical assessment

Right lower-quadrant pain and a nonvisualized appendix make this a genuine competing pathway. They do not resolve the simultaneous unlocated pregnancy/spotting problem; the supplied pelvic acquisition cannot establish that a pregnancy complication has been excluded. This does not prohibit subsequent surgical imaging or assessment.
Diagnostic uterine aspiration with histopathologic assessment

Falling hCG and bleeding can tempt a diagnosis of failed intrauterine pregnancy. Neither hCG nor the supplied scan establishes an intrauterine location or makes uterine sampling the immediate first diagnostic procedure in this record.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 47-year-old woman, visits for confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism after repeat calcium and parathyroid-hormone testing. Creatinine is within laboratory reference limits; renal ultrasound shows no calculi, and there is no fragility-fracture history. The referral requests an operative opinion and a baseline skeletal assessment.
before.Current update: The completed spine, hip and distal-radius bone-density measurements are within the age-appropriate reference range. Jamie Taylor has no hypercalcemic symptoms.
before.Task: Which management recommendation should be made for Jamie Taylor?
Options: Recommend biochemical surveillance through endocrinology follow-up
Recommend cinacalcet therapy through endocrinology follow-up

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 47-year-old woman, visits after repeat samples show calcium above the laboratory reference range and intact PTH within the reference range. An endocrine-surgery referral and baseline skeletal assessment were ordered at that visit. A prior DXA file contains the lumbar-spine acquisition. A right total hip replacement followed a high-energy injury; the left hip has native bone.
after.Current update: The completed lumbar-spine, native-left-hip and one-third-radius density measurements are within age-appropriate reference ranges. A paired serum and complete 24-hour urine collection gives a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01. Renal function and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are within reference ranges; there is no thiazide use. Earlier adult records show calcium in the same mildly elevated band, and the mother's records show a similar longstanding pattern.
after.Task: Which investigation should guide Jamie Taylor's parathyroid planning next?

before: **KEY:** Recommend parathyroidectomy through endocrine surgery

The patient remains younger than 50 in every retained presentation profile. That independent guideline criterion supports parathyroidectomy even when skeletal and renal assessment shows no complication. DXA characterizes baseline skeletal status; it does not create the age-based indication or have to become abnormal first.
Recommend biochemical surveillance through endocrinology follow-up

Monitoring is a genuine pathway when surgery is not selected, but normal organ assessment does not remove the independent age-based criterion in this patient. No contraindication or refusal of surgery has been introduced.
Recommend cinacalcet therapy through endocrinology follow-up

A named calcium-lowering medical pathway is more plausible than a generic bone-clinic foil. It does not replace discussion of an independently indicated operation in this represented, asymptomatic patient. This option teaches no medication dose or mandatory treatment algorithm.
after: **KEY:** Calcium-sensing receptor gene assay

The family/longitudinal pattern and low clearance ratio raise an inherited calcium-sensing disorder as a mimic of PHPT. The ratio supports that suspicion but does not confirm it. Genetic and family evaluation should clarify the disease before operative localization is treated as the remaining step. Normal DXA does not decide this distinction, and age under 50 is an operative criterion only after the relevant diagnosis is established. A negative CASR result would not exclude every suspected FHH case.
Parathyroid sestamibi scintigraphy

This is a credible next step if the clinician assumes that the biochemical pattern and young age have already settled PHPT and the need for localization. It would not resolve the inherited mimic raised by the urine/family record; localization is not a substitute for clarifying that diagnosis.
PTH-related peptide assay

A numerically reference-range intact PTH can tempt a different hypercalcemia workup. It does not exclude the recorded inherited calcium/PTH pattern, and this marker would not answer the family/genetic question supplied by the low urine ratio and longstanding familial findings.

packet.inference: Integrate the calcium/PTH, complete low-ratio collection and longstanding familial pattern as evidence of an inherited mimic rather than established PHPT. Then: Choose genetic clarification before localization; do not use young age or normal DXA to settle the diagnosis.
packet.focus: Low clearance ratio under interpretable collection conditions plus a longstanding similar maternal pattern; the biochemical pattern alone has not established PHPT.
packet.whatChanged: Removed specialty destinations and cinacalcet. Replaced an ambiguous draft operative-ranking comparison during self-check with a sourced inherited-calcium differential. The header now records the provisional raw biochemical pattern and an already-placed referral; the new concept tests genetic clarification before operative localization.

notes.note: Difficulty: the diagnosis is given and the decisive age rule is a single recall-to-recommendation step. after.Task: Using this audit, what approximate positive predictive value should be used for Jamie Taylor's reported PCR result?

before: **KEY:** About 70%
The specimen belongs to the pre-admission cohort, regardless of the later ICU care. Among that cohort's positive tests, 45 of 64 agree with the reference culture: 45/(45+19), about 70%.
About 92%
This is 180/(180+16), the positive predictive value of the ICU cohort. Applying it to a specimen collected in pre-admission screening imports the wrong tested population.
About 90%
This is sensitivity, 45/(45+5), not the proportion of positive screens that represent reference-confirmed carriage. Both cohorts have that same sensitivity.
About 5%
This is the pre-admission cohort's reference-positive fraction, (45+5)/1000. It is the pretest prevalence in the constructed audit, not the result-conditioned fraction.

after.Task: Which specimen plan should be requested next for Jamie Taylor's neck lymph node?

before: **KEY:** Core-needle biopsy with a peripheral solid-tissue target

The prior aspirate does not supply tissue architecture for classification. Sampling the solid, perfused portion with a core addresses both tissue adequacy and target selection; plasma EBV DNA cannot classify PTLD.
Fine-needle aspiration with a peripheral solid-tissue target

This targets a more representative part of the node, but repeats cytology when the unresolved question requires tissue for classification after the limited aspirate. The distinction is not a claim that FNA is never useful.
Core-needle biopsy with a central fluid-region target
This obtains a core in name but targets the fluid/debris component rather than the solid tissue needed for representative classification.
Fine-needle aspiration with a central fluid-region target
This would emphasize fluid/cellular material from the central component, leaving both the tissue-architecture and solid-target questions unresolved.
after: **KEY:** Excisional biopsy with fresh/fixed allocation

The accessible intact node can supply representative tissue for classification, while planned fresh and fixed portions allow the unresolved ancillary and histologic questions to be addressed. EBV detection and the limited aspirate do not classify the process.
Core biopsy with fresh/fixed allocation

This is the closest credible alternative and can be appropriate when excision is unsuitable. It corrects handling but provides a smaller specimen; the represented accessible node and unresolved tissue pattern favor the intended excisional plan.
Excisional biopsy with formalin fixation

This obtains intact tissue, but a wholly fixed specimen would not preserve a fresh sample for the unresolved flow-cytometry question. Choosing an excisional label does not by itself resolve specimen handling.
Core biopsy with formalin fixation
This combines a more limited tissue sample with fixation of the complete specimen. Both adequacy and the unresolved ancillary-study pathway require attention rather than a biopsy label in isolation.

concepts.displayName: Establish the early-pregnancy assessment pathway from discordant reassurance

concepts.displayName: Select valid hip and radial DXA acquisition regions in PHPT

concepts.displayName: Clarify inherited hypercalcemia before operative localization

concepts.displayName: Plan representative nodal tissue and ancillary handling after limited sampling
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret the prior same-target specimen and failed ancillary result, then combine a representative tissue method with processing that can answer the unresolved classification questions.

decisionNodes.stem: Before labeling {patientName}'s thrombocytopenia primary ITP, which testing should be arranged?
decisionNodes.explanation: HIV and hepatitis-C testing helps exclude secondary causes before concluding primary ITP, but negative serology alone does not establish the diagnosis.

resultGateAfter.resultNarrative: HIV and hepatitis-C testing are negative; the evaluation remains compatible with presumed primary ITP after the broader clinical review.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: HIV and hepatitis-C serology have returned negative. At this return visit, hemoglobin and the absolute neutrophil count are below their laboratory reference ranges. The smear describes macrocytic red cells and neutrophils with reduced granulation and fewer nuclear lobes. Vitamin B12 and folate are within reference ranges; the reticulocyte count is below range.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should precede another treatment recommendation for {patientName}'s thrombocytopenia?

answerChoices.label: Marrow aspirate and core biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The initial isolated platelet problem has become a multilineage cytopenia with altered cell morphology. Marrow assessment can examine production, morphology and tissue together before this is treated as another uncomplicated ITP relapse. The indication is the changed pattern, not the negative viral serology.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood flow cytometry assay
answerChoices.rationale: Flow cytometry is a credible investigation of an abnormal blood-cell population. Here the reported changes concern multiple lineages and maturation, and a blood immunophenotype would not supply the marrow morphology and tissue assessment underlying the intended next step. This is not a claim that flow studies have no role in the subsequent workup.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood myeloid sequencing assay
answerChoices.rationale: Molecular testing could contribute to classification, but a detected clone would not by itself establish the tissue/morphologic explanation of this changed cytopenia pattern. The near-miss is substituting a molecular result for the integrated marrow evaluation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which recommendation should be sent to {patientName}'s anesthesia team?

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; arrange contracture testing separately
answerChoices.rationale: The uneventful exposure and negative panel do not clear susceptibility in this family. With the represented nontriggering plan and documented MH preparation, definitive susceptibility testing need not become a prerequisite to surgery.

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; administer prophylactic dantrolene
answerChoices.rationale: This retains an appropriate intravenous technique but adds prophylaxis as though familial risk requires pretreatment even with trigger avoidance and MH preparation. It confuses readiness to treat a crisis with routinely administering the rescue drug.

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia after muscle-contracture testing
answerChoices.rationale: The family result and negative panel justify continued risk precautions, not necessarily delaying surgery until a definitive susceptibility test is completed. This is a credible sequencing error when an inconclusive genetic result is treated as a barrier to a nontriggering anesthetic.

decisionNodes.stem: Which radiology request should be made at this visit for {patientName}'s persistent palpable finding?

answerChoices.label: Request targeted breast ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: The complete acquisition record corresponds to the other marker, not the persistent lower-inner finding. Targeted imaging should be correlated with the current palpable site. This requests a different acquisition rather than simply repeating an adequate study.

answerChoices.label: Request archived breast ultrasound images
answerChoices.rationale: Retrieval is a credible near-miss when an acquisition exists but transferred images are missing. The complete recorded acquisition here addresses the other marker, so retrieving that accession would not supply the required clinical-site correlation.

answerChoices.label: Request spot-compression breast mammography
answerChoices.rationale: This would be reasonable if the mammographic acquisition did not cover the current marker. The supplied views already include it; the unresolved issue is targeted sonographic correlation with the actual clinical finding, not another mammographic view.

decisionNodes.stem: Which same-day diagnostic plan should be prioritized for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Transvaginal ultrasonography with gynecologic assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The early home result, falling but detectable hCG and transabdominal scan do not establish pregnancy location. The new focal symptoms require prompt assessment of an early-pregnancy complication rather than a conclusion of completed miscarriage or a settled appendiceal diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Appendiceal MRI with general-surgical assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Right lower-quadrant pain and a nonvisualized appendix make this a genuine competing pathway. They do not resolve the simultaneous unlocated pregnancy/spotting problem; the supplied pelvic acquisition cannot establish that a pregnancy complication has been excluded. This does not prohibit subsequent surgical imaging or assessment.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic uterine aspiration with histopathologic assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Falling hCG and bleeding can tempt a diagnosis of failed intrauterine pregnancy. Neither hCG nor the supplied scan establishes an intrauterine location or makes uterine sampling the immediate first diagnostic procedure in this record.

answerChoices.label: Left hip and distal one-third radius

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should guide {patientName}'s parathyroid planning next?

answerChoices.label: Calcium-sensing receptor gene assay
answerChoices.rationale: The family/longitudinal pattern and low clearance ratio raise an inherited calcium-sensing disorder as a mimic of PHPT. The ratio supports that suspicion but does not confirm it. Genetic and family evaluation should clarify the disease before operative localization is treated as the remaining step. Normal DXA does not decide this distinction, and age under 50 is an operative criterion only after the relevant diagnosis is established. A negative CASR result would not exclude every suspected FHH case.

answerChoices.label: Parathyroid sestamibi scintigraphy
answerChoices.rationale: This is a credible next step if the clinician assumes that the biochemical pattern and young age have already settled PHPT and the need for localization. It would not resolve the inherited mimic raised by the urine/family record; localization is not a substitute for clarifying that diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: PTH-related peptide assay
answerChoices.rationale: A numerically reference-range intact PTH can tempt a different hypercalcemia workup. It does not exclude the recorded inherited calcium/PTH pattern, and this marker would not answer the family/genetic question supplied by the low urine ratio and longstanding familial findings.

decisionNodes.stem: Using this audit, what approximate positive predictive value should be used for {patientName}'s reported PCR result?

answerChoices.label: About 70%
answerChoices.rationale: The specimen belongs to the pre-admission cohort, regardless of the later ICU care. Among that cohort's positive tests, 45 of 64 agree with the reference culture: 45/(45+19), about 70%.

answerChoices.label: About 92%
answerChoices.rationale: This is 180/(180+16), the positive predictive value of the ICU cohort. Applying it to a specimen collected in pre-admission screening imports the wrong tested population.

answerChoices.label: About 90%
answerChoices.rationale: This is sensitivity, 45/(45+5), not the proportion of positive screens that represent reference-confirmed carriage. Both cohorts have that same sensitivity.

answerChoices.label: About 5%
answerChoices.rationale: This is the pre-admission cohort's reference-positive fraction, (45+5)/1000. It is the pretest prevalence in the constructed audit, not the result-conditioned fraction.

decisionNodes.stem: Which specimen plan should be requested next for {patientName}'s neck lymph node?

answerChoices.label: Excisional biopsy with fresh/fixed allocation
answerChoices.rationale: The accessible intact node can supply representative tissue for classification, while planned fresh and fixed portions allow the unresolved ancillary and histologic questions to be addressed. EBV detection and the limited aspirate do not classify the process.

answerChoices.label: Core biopsy with fresh/fixed allocation
answerChoices.rationale: This is the closest credible alternative and can be appropriate when excision is unsuitable. It corrects handling but provides a smaller specimen; the represented accessible node and unresolved tissue pattern favor the intended excisional plan.

answerChoices.label: Excisional biopsy with formalin fixation
answerChoices.rationale: This obtains intact tissue, but a wholly fixed specimen would not preserve a fresh sample for the unresolved flow-cytometry question. Choosing an excisional label does not by itself resolve specimen handling.

answerChoices.label: Core biopsy with formalin fixation
answerChoices.rationale: This combines a more limited tissue sample with fixation of the complete specimen. Both adequacy and the unresolved ancillary-study pathway require attention rather than a biopsy label in isolation.

definitions.previousCurrentUpdate: The returned HIV and hepatitis-C serology is negative. Platelet counts since the relapse have remained above 30 × 10^9/L. Bruises have recurred, but there has been no mucosal or internal bleeding. Hematology is continuing treatment and follow-up; {patientName} asks about an operation after the relapse.
definitions.currentUpdate: HIV and hepatitis-C serology have returned negative. At this return visit, hemoglobin and the absolute neutrophil count are below their laboratory reference ranges. The smear describes macrocytic red cells and neutrophils with reduced granulation and fewer nuclear lobes. Vitamin B12 and folate are within reference ranges; the reticulocyte count is below range.
definitions.intendedInference: Compare the current blood-cell pattern with the initially isolated thrombocytopenia. Then: Choose an investigation that evaluates the new production/morphology problem rather than substituting a blood immunophenotype or molecular clone for tissue assessment.
definitions.reviewerNotes: Key hold: directly verify the ITP-consensus changed-cytopenia/marrow boundary and comparative workup with hematology before acceptance. The existing claim covers isolated-thrombocytopenia evaluation, not this full marrow-versus-flow-versus-sequencing ranking. No exact one-year rule or automatic HIV/HCV-to-marrow sequence is taught.

question.stem: Which investigation should precede another treatment recommendation for {patientName}'s thrombocytopenia?

answerChoices.label: Marrow aspirate and core biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The initial isolated platelet problem has become a multilineage cytopenia with altered cell morphology. Marrow assessment can examine production, morphology and tissue together before this is treated as another uncomplicated ITP relapse. The indication is the changed pattern, not the negative viral serology.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood flow cytometry assay
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Flow cytometry is a credible investigation of an abnormal blood-cell population. Here the reported changes concern multiple lineages and maturation, and a blood immunophenotype would not supply the marrow morphology and tissue assessment underlying the intended next step. This is not a claim that flow studies have no role in the subsequent workup.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood myeloid sequencing assay
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Molecular testing could contribute to classification, but a detected clone would not by itself establish the tissue/morphologic explanation of this changed cytopenia pattern. The near-miss is substituting a molecular result for the integrated marrow evaluation.

question.stem: Which recommendation should be sent to {patientName}'s anesthesia team?

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; arrange contracture testing separately
answerChoices.rationale: The uneventful exposure and negative panel do not clear susceptibility in this family. With the represented nontriggering plan and documented MH preparation, definitive susceptibility testing need not become a prerequisite to surgery.

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; administer prophylactic dantrolene
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This retains an appropriate intravenous technique but adds prophylaxis as though familial risk requires pretreatment even with trigger avoidance and MH preparation. It confuses readiness to treat a crisis with routinely administering the rescue drug.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: The family result and negative panel justify continued risk precautions, not necessarily delaying surgery until a definitive susceptibility test is completed. This is a credible sequencing error when an inconclusive genetic result is treated as a barrier to a nontriggering anesthetic.

concepts.displayName: Select valid hip and radial DXA acquisition regions in PHPT
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret the acquired lumbar series and hip hardware record, then combine a valid native-hip site with the PHPT forearm region.
concepts.versioningReason: Replaces routine modality recall with acquisition adequacy in a patient-specific hardware context. Preserve the old three-site-baseline card and keep operative consultation independent of the game result gate.

concepts.displayName: Clarify inherited hypercalcemia before operative localization
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret calcium/PTH, relative hypocalciuria and family/longitudinal findings, then pursue genetic clarification instead of assuming that young age establishes PHPT or that localization can establish its diagnosis.
concepts.versioningReason: Changes age-rule recall into a diagnostic-sequencing application that changes the operative pathway. Preserve the original age-based indication card. The new header records a provisional biochemical workup/referral and the later family/urine record raises an inherited mimic; DXA remains baseline characterization, not eligibility permission.

concepts.displayName: Plan representative nodal tissue and ancillary handling after limited sampling
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret the prior same-target specimen and failed ancillary result, then combine a representative tissue method with processing that can answer the unresolved classification questions.
concepts.versioningReason: Changes round one's solid-versus-fluid target selection into tissue-method and handling planning. Both methods target the same solid node, prior target is explicit, and historical coordination/target cards remain intact.

answerChoices.rationale: Site relates to both intervention use and the outcome, and the comparison ignores it. Their mixed association is the stated confounding concern.

answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit describes an ignored third factor in the comparison, not differential entry into the sample. That is the confounding rather than selection mechanism supplied.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit describes an ignored third factor in the comparison, not differential entry into the sample. That is the confounding rather than selection mechanism supplied.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: No unequal recall or outcome-recording method is described. The stated problem is the ignored relationship of site with both exposure and outcome.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit does not describe unequal recall. It describes exclusion of nighttime surgical patients from an all-patients conclusion.

answerChoices.label: Random error from insufficient sample precision
answerChoices.rationale: A large daytime sample can still exclude the target population of nighttime surgical patients. Greater sampling precision does not repair that selection problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A large daytime sample can still exclude the target population of nighttime surgical patients. Greater sampling precision does not repair that selection problem.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.teachingPoint: Selection bias concerns which observations enter the study. A large daytime-only sample still leaves nighttime surgical patients outside an audit presented as applying to all eligible surgical patients. Sample size cannot repair that missing coverage. Distinguish this selection problem from confounding within the comparison or inconsistent measurement after people have entered it.

One group reported thrombotic events when they occurred; another recalled events six months later. A colleague points out that everyone used the same form. The investigators are reviewing the collection process, and the report specifies how the two reporting schedules differed during follow-up.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.stem: Which information problem most directly threatens the outcome comparison when one group reports immediately and the other recalls events six months later?

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from unequal recall
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate recording in one group and recall six months later in the other use unequal measurement processes. That can systematically distort the recorded contrast.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: The difference concerns how outcomes were recorded after entry, rather than how people were selected for the study.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The difference concerns how outcomes were recorded after entry, rather than how people were selected for the study.

answerChoices.label: Confounding by baseline study site
answerChoices.rationale: No baseline site factor is supplied as relating exposure and the outcome. The stated concern is the unequal reporting schedule.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No baseline site factor is supplied as relating exposure and the outcome. The stated concern is the unequal reporting schedule.

answerChoices.label: Random error from natural variation
answerChoices.rationale: The groups are measured by different recall processes. That systematic difference is not simply random variation that a larger sample necessarily removes.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The groups are measured by different recall processes. That systematic difference is not simply random variation that a larger sample necessarily removes.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.explanation: The primary concern is measurement bias from unequal recall schedules. The groups' recorded outcomes may differ because one reports immediately and the other recalls much later.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.teachingPoint: Measurement bias can arise when groups' outcomes are recorded differently. Immediate reports and recall six months later use unequal measurement processes, so a difference in reports may reflect how the outcomes were remembered. This is distinct from who was recruited or which baseline factor confounds the comparison. Larger samples do not equalize the reporting methods.

The reporting schedules differ; no real device effect is supplied. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the anesthesia journal-club lead, reviews a new monitoring sensor for malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility. An observational model compares recognition of concerning intraoperative changes. Investigators adjusted for recorded differences between groups. Follow-up access relates to both sensor choice and recorded recognition, but important access differences were not measured. The report describes those stipulated relationships and the model under review.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.stem: Which limitation remains after adjustment when an important factor related to both sensor choice and recorded outcomes was not measured?

answerChoices.label: Residual confounding by unmeasured factors
answerChoices.rationale: Unrecorded follow-up access differences relate to intervention choice and the outcome. Adjustment for other factors leaves that potential confounding unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Random error from the sampling process
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit identifies an unrecorded associated factor, not just sampling variability. Greater precision would not supply the missing follow-up access information.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit identifies an unrecorded associated factor, not just sampling variability. Greater precision would not supply the missing follow-up access information.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: No enrollment mechanism is described as the primary concern. The known limitation is confounding by follow-up access differences absent from the model.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No enrollment mechanism is described as the primary concern. The known limitation is confounding by follow-up access differences absent from the model.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from inconsistent outcome recording
answerChoices.rationale: No inconsistent outcome-recording process is supplied. The gap is a relevant factor the model could not adjust for because it was not recorded.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No inconsistent outcome-recording process is supplied. The gap is a relevant factor the model could not adjust for because it was not recorded.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.explanation: Residual confounding remains because relevant follow-up access differences were not measured. Adjusting for site and procedure category does not automatically account for that unrecorded factor.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.teachingPoint: Adjustment can address recorded factors without accounting for unrecorded ones. Follow-up access still relates to both intervention choice and the outcome, so residual confounding remains possible despite adjustment for site and procedure category. Remember that an adjusted label is not a guarantee of an unconfounded result; ask which relevant differences the model could actually use.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.stem: How does the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's positive predictive value change between the hypothetical populations when sensitivity and specificity remain fixed as stated?

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value increases
answerChoices.rationale: With sensitivity and specificity fixed, the higher-prevalence population has a greater true-positive share among positive screens. This supports an increase, without an exact percentage.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value decreases
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction: higher prevalence increases the true-positive share among positives under the fixed-test assumptions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the direction: higher prevalence increases the true-positive share among positives under the fixed-test assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value stays fixed
answerChoices.rationale: Fixed sensitivity and specificity do not fix positive predictive value. Prevalence also determines the mix of true and false positives.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Fixed sensitivity and specificity do not fix positive predictive value. Prevalence also determines the mix of true and false positives.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value is indeterminate
answerChoices.rationale: An exact percentage would need more numbers, but the direction follows from higher prevalence with fixed test characteristics. That direction is not indeterminate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An exact percentage would need more numbers, but the direction follows from higher prevalence with fixed test characteristics. That direction is not indeterminate.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.explanation: Positive predictive value increases under the stated fixed-test assumptions because prevalence is higher. The exhibit supports the direction of change without supplying an exact personal probability.
question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.teachingPoint: Positive predictive value asks what share of positive results come from people with the condition. With sensitivity and specificity held fixed, higher prevalence makes true positives a larger share of positives, so predictive value rises. Remember that the test and the tested population both matter; this comparison gives direction, not a personal percentage.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.stem: Which difference can explain the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's different positive predictive values when testing definitions, sensitivity and specificity remain the same?

answerChoices.label: Different prevalence in the tested populations
answerChoices.rationale: Prevalence can change the true-positive share among positive results even with identical testing processes, sensitivity, and specificity. It is a possible explanation, not an exact value.

answerChoices.label: Different sensitivity in the tested populations
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit explicitly keeps sensitivity the same. A sensitivity difference cannot explain this exercise without contradicting that condition.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit explicitly keeps sensitivity the same. A sensitivity difference cannot explain this exercise without contradicting that condition.

answerChoices.label: Different specificity in the tested populations
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit explicitly keeps specificity the same. This proposed explanation changes an assumption that was held fixed.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit explicitly keeps specificity the same. This proposed explanation changes an assumption that was held fixed.

answerChoices.label: Different definitions of a positive test result
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit keeps the testing process and definition of positive the same. Reclassifying results contradicts that supplied comparison.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit keeps the testing process and definition of positive the same. Reclassifying results contradicts that supplied comparison.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.explanation: Different prevalence can produce different positive predictive values despite identical test characteristics. The exhibit explicitly holds sensitivity, specificity, and result definitions constant.
question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.teachingPoint: Sensitivity and specificity describe results within condition-status groups; positive predictive value starts with positive results. Changing prevalence can change the mix of true and false positives even when those test characteristics stay fixed. Here prevalence is a possible explanation. The information does not supply its exact value or prove a personal diagnosis.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the biliary journal-club lead, reviews a new dissection instrument for acute cholecystitis operations. The observational study reports surgical-site infection within thirty days. Its sponsor requests a balanced account: equal space for the data and the company's response to the data. The report supplies risks in exposed and unexposed groups, and the team is reviewing the comparison.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: What risk ratio compares exposed with unexposed participants for the clinical outcome in the constructed cohort?

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: Divide exposed risk by unexposed risk: 0.20/0.10 = 2.0. The inputs are probabilities, so the result is a risk ratio.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: The quotient 0.20/0.10 compares risks, not odds. Calling that number an odds ratio changes the scale without doing an odds calculation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The quotient 0.20/0.10 compares risks, not odds. Calling that number an odds ratio changes the scale without doing an odds calculation.

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: The value 0.5 comes from 0.10/0.20, reversing the requested exposed-versus-unexposed direction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The value 0.5 comes from 0.10/0.20, reversing the requested exposed-versus-unexposed direction.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: This both reverses the comparison and assigns an odds label to a calculation of probabilities. Neither change preserves the requested estimate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This both reverses the comparison and assigns an odds label to a calculation of probabilities. Neither change preserves the requested estimate.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: Dividing the exposed risk by the unexposed risk gives 0.20/0.10 = 2.0, a risk ratio. That calculation does not become an odds ratio by relabeling it.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: Risk is a probability; a risk ratio divides one group's probability by the comparator's. Here 20%/10% = 2.0 for exposed versus unexposed over 30 days. An odds ratio compares odds instead. Remember both the scale and direction: reversing the groups gives a reciprocal, while changing the label changes the claimed measure.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: Which association measure can be calculated directly from the case-control exposure table for postoperative leak?

answerChoices.label: Exposure odds ratio of 1.8
answerChoices.rationale: Compare exposure odds in cases and controls: (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8. This gives an exposure odds ratio for the supplied outcome-selected sample.

answerChoices.label: Exposure risk ratio of 1.8
answerChoices.rationale: The sampling plan selects cases and controls by outcome. Their totals do not provide the population risks needed to justify a risk-ratio label.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The sampling plan selects cases and controls by outcome. Their totals do not provide the population risks needed to justify a risk-ratio label.

answerChoices.label: Exposure odds ratio of 0.56
answerChoices.rationale: About 0.56 is the reciprocal of 1.8. It describes controls versus cases, reversing the requested exposure-odds comparison.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: About 0.56 is the reciprocal of 1.8. It describes controls versus cases, reversing the requested exposure-odds comparison.

answerChoices.label: Exposure risk ratio of 0.56
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction and uses a risk scale unsupported by the outcome-selected sampling totals.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the direction and uses a risk scale unsupported by the outcome-selected sampling totals.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: The exposure odds ratio is (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8 for cases versus controls. Population risks are not supplied, so a risk-ratio label is unsupported.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: In this outcome-selected table, compare exposure odds in cases with exposure odds in controls: (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8. That is an exposure odds ratio. The sampled case and control totals do not supply population event risks. Remember what the design selected before deciding whether a risk-ratio label is justified.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the skin-oncology discussion lead, reviews a new biologic for Merkel cell carcinoma. An adjusted model reports recurrence odds over two years. The representative offers to simplify the statistics by removing the parts customers ask about. question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: How should the adjusted odds ratio of 0.60 for two-year recurrence be described when group risks are unavailable?

answerChoices.label: Adjusted odds are 0.60 times as high
answerChoices.rationale: The reported adjusted odds ratio is 0.60. Describing the adjusted odds as 0.60 times the comparison odds keeps the estimate on its reported scale.

answerChoices.label: Adjusted risk is exactly 0.60 times as high
answerChoices.rationale: The model reports odds, not an exact ratio of probabilities. Group risks needed for that asserted risk comparison are not supplied.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The model reports odds, not an exact ratio of probabilities. Group risks needed for that asserted risk comparison are not supplied.

answerChoices.label: Absolute risk falls by 40 percentage points
answerChoices.rationale: An odds ratio alone does not provide an absolute risk difference. Subtracting it from one cannot create a 40-percentage-point reduction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An odds ratio alone does not provide an absolute risk difference. Subtracting it from one cannot create a 40-percentage-point reduction.

answerChoices.label: Adjusted event probability is 40% lower
answerChoices.rationale: An odds ratio of 0.60 cannot automatically be translated into a 40% reduction in event probability. That changes odds into risk without the needed information.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An odds ratio of 0.60 cannot automatically be translated into a 40% reduction in event probability. That changes odds into risk without the needed information.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: The estimate describes adjusted odds at 0.60 times the comparison odds. Without group risks, it cannot provide the asserted exact risk ratio or absolute risk reduction.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: Odds and probability are different scales. An adjusted odds ratio of 0.60 says the compared odds are 0.60 times the reference odds, within the reported model. It does not supply the same proportional probability reduction or an absolute risk difference. Keep the measure's name attached to its number when translating a report.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the bariatric journal-club lead, reviews a new protective agent for marginal ulcer after gastric bypass. The observational report labels its estimate as an exposure odds ratio for rare ulcer recurrence. The editor requests a more exciting conclusion while retaining 'strictly factual.' Underlying group risks are unavailable, and the investigators discuss approximate similarity to a risk ratio.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: Which interpretation preserves the reported measure when an exposure odds ratio for rare ulcer recurrence is discussed as approximately similar to a risk ratio?

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as an odds ratio
answerChoices.rationale: The report actually estimates an odds ratio. Retaining its label preserves the measure despite the stated approximate similarity for this rare outcome.

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as a relative risk
answerChoices.rationale: Approximate similarity does not establish an exact risk ratio. Baseline risks for a direct risk comparison are not supplied.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Approximate similarity does not establish an exact risk ratio. Baseline risks for a direct risk comparison are not supplied.

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as a relative risk reduction
answerChoices.rationale: A relative risk reduction is a different claim from the reported odds ratio. The supplied information does not justify relabeling the measure that way.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A relative risk reduction is a different claim from the reported odds ratio. The supplied information does not justify relabeling the measure that way.

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as an absolute risk difference
answerChoices.rationale: An absolute risk difference requires probabilities to subtract. The reported odds ratio and missing baseline risks do not supply those values.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An absolute risk difference requires probabilities to subtract. The reported odds ratio and missing baseline risks do not supply those values.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: Report the estimate as an odds ratio. The stated approximate similarity does not convert it into an exact risk ratio or supply an absolute risk difference.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: Approximate similarity is not permission to rename an estimate. The report gives an odds ratio, so retain that label even when discussing a rare outcome. Without the underlying risks, the exhibit does not supply an exact risk ratio or an absolute difference. A useful reporting rule is to preserve the scale you actually estimated.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v1.stem: For colon-cancer recurrence over two years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Subtracting gives 0.10; 1/0.10 = 10 for the specified outcome over two years.

answerChoices.label: ARR 50 percentage points; NNT 2 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The outcome risk halves relative to its 20% starting value, but falls by 10 percentage points, not 50. The relative wording does not supply this ARR or NNT.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The outcome risk halves relative to its 20% starting value, but falls by 10 percentage points, not 50. The relative wording does not supply this ARR or NNT.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 100 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The absolute difference is right, but its reciprocal uses the proportion 0.10: 1/0.10 = 10, not 100.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The absolute difference is right, but its reciprocal uses the proportion 0.10: 1/0.10 = 10, not 100.

answerChoices.label: ARR 5 percentage points; NNT 20 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: An NNT of 20 would correspond to an absolute difference of 0.05. These practice risks differ by 0.10 instead.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An NNT of 20 would correspond to an absolute difference of 0.05. These practice risks differ by 0.10 instead.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v1.explanation: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Their difference is 0.10, giving ARR 10 percentage points and NNT 10 for the specified two-year outcome.
question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v1.teachingPoint: Calculate each group's risk first, then subtract intervention risk from comparator risk. Here 20% minus 10% is 10 percentage points, so NNT is 1/0.10 = 10 over two years. Half the starting risk and a 10-point absolute drop describe the same practice numbers; keep the outcome, comparator, and period attached.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v2.stem: For cutaneous-SCC recurrence over three years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 5 percentage points; NNT 20 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: First divide within each group: 30/200 = 0.15 and 10/100 = 0.10. ARR is 0.05 and its reciprocal is NNT 20 over three years.

answerChoices.label: ARR 20 percentage points; NNT 5 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: Subtracting 30 and 10 events ignores that the groups contain 200 and 100 people. Risks, rather than raw counts, must be subtracted.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Subtracting 30 and 10 events ignores that the groups contain 200 and 100 people. Risks, rather than raw counts, must be subtracted.

answerChoices.label: ARR 33 percentage points; NNT 3 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: About 33% describes the relative reduction from 15% to 10%. The absolute drop is five percentage points, giving NNT 20.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: About 33% describes the relative reduction from 15% to 10%. The absolute drop is five percentage points, giving NNT 20.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: The comparator risk is 30/200 = 15%, not 20%. Using the actual denominator gives a five-point difference rather than ten.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The comparator risk is 30/200 = 15%, not 20%. Using the actual denominator gives a five-point difference rather than ten.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v2.explanation: First calculate risks: 30/200 = 0.15 and 10/100 = 0.10. ARR is 0.05, or five percentage points, and three-year NNT is 20.
question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v2.teachingPoint: Unequal group sizes make raw event-count subtraction misleading. Convert each count to a risk: 30/200 = 15% and 10/100 = 10%. Their absolute difference is five percentage points, so NNT is 1/0.05 = 20 over three years. Remember: divide within groups before subtracting between groups, retaining the specified recurrence outcome and comparator.

answerChoices.rationale: Subtract 10/100 from 30/100 to get 0.20. The reciprocal is 1/0.20 = 5 for the same comparator and five-year outcome.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over five years

answerChoices.distractorRationale: The two practice risks are 30% and 10%, a 20-point difference. A ten-point reduction would describe different inputs.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v3.explanation: The practice outcome risks differ by 0.30 - 0.10 = 0.20. ARR is 20 percentage points and NNT is 5 over the stated five-year period.
question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v3.teachingPoint: Absolute reduction subtracts risks on the same scale: 30% minus 10% is 20 percentage points. Taking the reciprocal of 0.20 gives NNT 5 for this comparator and outcome over five years. The relative reduction uses a different starting denominator. Remember that percentage points, percentages, and proportions are not interchangeable labels.

answerChoices.label: ARR 14 percentage points; NNT 8 over two years

Then 1/0.06 is about 16.67; conventionally round NNT upward to 17. Keep the specified recurrence outcome, comparator, and two-year period with the result. The trial compares thirty-day surgical-site infection and reports its preplanned analysis. Investigators specified the null model before collecting outcomes. The team has the p-value but is reviewing what that value says about the infection results before drafting the study's written conclusion.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v1.stem: Which interpretation is justified by the reported p-value for thirty-day SSI in the constructed trial?

answerChoices.label: A 3% chance of results this extreme or more under the null model
answerChoices.rationale: Assume the specified null model and analysis conditions. Results this incompatible with that model, or more so, have probability 0.03; the probability is conditional on the model.

answerChoices.label: A 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the conditioning. The p-value assumes the null model to evaluate data, rather than assigning a 3% probability to the null hypothesis after observing data.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the conditioning. The p-value assumes the null model to evaluate data, rather than assigning a 3% probability to the null hypothesis after observing data.

answerChoices.label: A 97% probability that the intervention truly changed the outcome after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: One minus p does not supply a posterior probability that the intervention truly changed scores. The complement 0.97 is not that truth probability.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: One minus p does not supply a posterior probability that the intervention truly changed scores. The complement 0.97 is not that truth probability.

answerChoices.label: An estimated difference of 0.03 outcome units between the two groups being compared
answerChoices.rationale: The 0.03 is a probability under a null model, not a difference in outcome units. Read the effect magnitude from its separately reported estimate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The 0.03 is a probability under a null model, not a difference in outcome units. Read the effect magnitude from its separately reported estimate.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v1.explanation: Under the specified null model, results this extreme or more have probability 0.03. That is neither the probability of a true null nor the size of the clinical difference.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v1.teachingPoint: A null model is the comparison's starting assumption. A p-value asks how probable data this incompatible with that model, or more so, would be under the model and analysis conditions. Here that probability is 0.03. Remember: probability of data under a model is not probability that the model is true, and is not effect size.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational gallbladder dissection instrument trial: invented analysis of thirty-day SSI for practice. The null specifies no group difference; the p-value is not an effect size or personal outcome probability.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v2.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the colorectal research lead, reviews a new fixation technique for rectal prolapse and recurrence within two years. The press officer wants a headline saying the study settled the issue; the statistician has been offered a footnote in exchange for missing the press conference. The report includes its preplanned null model and the p-value from that analysis.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v2.stem: Which interpretation is justified by the reported p-value for two-year recurrence in the constructed trial?

answerChoices.label: A 40% chance of results this extreme or more under the null model
answerChoices.rationale: The 0.40 is the probability of data this extreme or more under the specified null model and its analysis assumptions. A larger number retains the same conditioning.

answerChoices.label: A 40% probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: A p-value does not estimate the probability that the null is true. The 0.40 concerns data calculated assuming the null model.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A p-value does not estimate the probability that the null is true. The 0.40 concerns data calculated assuming the null model.

answerChoices.label: A 60% probability that no group difference exists after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: Subtracting p from one gives 0.60 arithmetically, but does not make that the probability of no effect.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Subtracting p from one gives 0.60 arithmetically, but does not make that the probability of no effect.

answerChoices.label: An estimated difference of 0.40 outcome units between the two groups being compared
answerChoices.rationale: A probability under the null model is not a 0.40-unit outcome difference. Effect magnitude requires its own estimate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A probability under the null model is not a 0.40-unit outcome difference. Effect magnitude requires its own estimate.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v2.explanation: The 0.40 describes data at least this extreme under the specified null model. It does not assign 40% or 60% probability to a hypothesis or quantify the effect.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v2.teachingPoint: The null model supplies a starting comparison assumption. A p-value describes the probability of data this extreme or more if that model and its analysis assumptions hold. Here that probability is 0.40. Neither p nor one minus p gives the probability of no effect. Effect size requires a separate estimate.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational rectal-prolapse fixation technique trial: invented analysis of two-year recurrence for practice. The null specifies no group difference; the p-value is not an effect size or personal outcome probability.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v3.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the gastric-oncology discussion lead, reviews a new agent for gastric MALT lymphoma in an invented recurrence-prevention trial after remission. Follow-up lasts two years. The sponsor requests 'life-changing' on every slide, including the Wi-Fi password. The trial reports a very small p-value, with its effect estimate supplied separately; the team is reviewing the interpretation for its report.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v3.stem: Which interpretation is justified by the reported p-value for two-year lymphoma recurrence in the constructed trial?

answerChoices.label: A 0.1% chance of results this extreme or more under the null model
answerChoices.rationale: Under the specified null model and conditions, data this incompatible or more have probability 0.001. The small value does not change what the probability describes.

answerChoices.label: A 0.1% probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: The test assumes the null model when calculating this probability; it does not assign 0.001 probability to the null hypothesis itself.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The test assumes the null model when calculating this probability; it does not assign 0.001 probability to the null hypothesis itself.

answerChoices.label: A 99.9% probability that the intervention truly changed the outcome after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: The complement 0.999 is not a posterior probability that an effect is true. That interpretation does not follow from the reported p-value.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The complement 0.999 is not a posterior probability that an effect is true. That interpretation does not follow from the reported p-value.

answerChoices.label: An estimated difference of 0.001 outcome units between the two groups being compared
answerChoices.rationale: The number 0.001 is a probability, not an effect in outcome units. The exhibit says the effect estimate is reported separately.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The number 0.001 is a probability, not an effect in outcome units. The exhibit says the effect estimate is reported separately.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v3.explanation: The 0.001 refers to data under the specified null model, including more extreme results. It is not a posterior truth probability or the effect estimate.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v3.teachingPoint: A null model is a starting comparison assumption, not the conclusion. Under that model and its assumptions, results at least this incompatible have probability 0.001. A small p-value does not make the effect 0.001 units or assign 0.999 probability to its truth. Read magnitude from the separately reported estimate.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v4.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the emergency-surgery journal-club lead, reviews a new anastomosis instrument after ileal resection for symptomatic Meckel diverticulum. The trial records leak within thirty days. Its analysis does not reject the prespecified null model, and a draft conclusion says the instruments have exactly equal effects. The report gives the p-value and that proposed conclusion for the team's discussion.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v4.stem: Which interpretation is justified by the reported p-value for thirty-day leak in the constructed trial?

answerChoices.label: The result does not prove exact equality
answerChoices.rationale: The p-value does not prove a zero group difference. The exact-equality sentence claims more than the reported probability establishes.

answerChoices.label: The result favors equal group effects
answerChoices.rationale: Failure to establish a difference is not proof or a supplied probability of equality. The p-value alone does not settle whether the means are exactly equal.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Failure to establish a difference is not proof or a supplied probability of equality. The p-value alone does not settle whether the means are exactly equal.

answerChoices.label: The result indicates a small clinical difference
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit supplies no effect magnitude or clinical-importance criterion. A p-value alone cannot establish a small clinical difference.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit supplies no effect magnitude or clinical-importance criterion. A p-value alone cannot establish a small clinical difference.

answerChoices.label: The result gives an 8% probability of no effect
answerChoices.rationale: The 0.08 describes data conditional on a null model, not an 8% probability that no effect exists after observing the data.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The 0.08 describes data conditional on a null model, not an 8% probability that no effect exists after observing the data.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v4.explanation: The reported p-value does not prove exact equality. It also does not give an 8% probability of no effect or establish that any difference is clinically small.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v4.teachingPoint: A null model is a starting comparison assumption; a p-value describes data under that model. It does not establish exact group equality, the probability of no effect, or the clinical size of a difference. Remember the boundary: this number alone cannot certify equality, magnitude, or clinical importance.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational Meckel resection anastomosis instrument trial: invented analysis of thirty-day leak for practice. The null specifies no group difference; the p-value is not an effect size or personal outcome probability.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the groin-surgery research lead, reviews a new reinforcement material for femoral hernia repair. The trial reports recurrence within two years as a risk ratio with an interval. The sponsor welcomes uncertainty in principle, but asks whether it can be moved to the appendix. The team is reviewing how the reported range relates to the no-difference value.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.stem: How does the constructed two-year recurrence risk-ratio interval relate to its null value, and what interpretation is justified?

answerChoices.label: The interval includes the null value 1
answerChoices.rationale: One lies between 0.40 and 1.20, so the interval includes the no-association value for a ratio. Inclusion does not establish an exactly true ratio of one.

answerChoices.label: The interval excludes the null value 1
answerChoices.rationale: The upper limit is 1.20 and the lower limit is 0.40. One is inside these limits, so it is not excluded.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The upper limit is 1.20 and the lower limit is 0.40. One is inside these limits, so it is not excluded.

answerChoices.label: The interval gives 95% probability of a real association
answerChoices.rationale: The 95% level describes coverage of the interval method. It does not give a 95% probability that an association is real.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The 95% level describes coverage of the interval method. It does not give a 95% probability that an association is real.

answerChoices.label: The interval supports an exactly absent association
answerChoices.rationale: An interval containing one is compatible with the ratio null value, but also contains other ratios. It does not prove that the association is exactly absent.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An interval containing one is compatible with the ratio null value, but also contains other ratios. It does not prove that the association is exactly absent.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.explanation: The ratio interval from 0.40 to 1.20 contains 1. It is compatible with the ratio null value, without proving an exactly absent association.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.teachingPoint: For a ratio, the no-association value is 1, because the compared quantities are equal. One falls within 0.40 to 1.20, so this interval includes that null value. Inclusion is not proof that the true ratio is exactly 1. Remember the measure's scale before looking for its null value.
