answerChoices.distractorRationale: Large rod-like calcifications are categorized as typically benign.

answerChoices.label: Coarse, densely calcified, confluent calcifications
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This coarse densely calcified profile is categorized as typically benign.

question.breast-imaging.calcification.se.explanation: Suspicious fine linear or branching morphology combined with a segmental distribution is the most concerning profile in this answer set.

question.breast-imaging.calcification.se.patientPresentation: A patient brings a completed mammography report that lists several possible calcification descriptors. The task is to identify the suspicious morphology.
question.breast-imaging.calcification.se.stem: Which calcification morphology is categorized as suspicious on mammography?

answerChoices.label: Vascular calcifications
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vascular calcifications are categorized as typically benign.

answerChoices.label: Rim calcifications
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Rim calcifications are categorized as typically benign.

answerChoices.label: Layering calcifications
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Layering calcifications are categorized as typically benign.

question.breast-imaging.calcification.se.explanation: Fine pleomorphic morphology is suspicious; the other listed patterns are categorized as typically benign.

question.breast-imaging.calcification.se.patientPresentation: A patient is seen after mammography has identified breast calcifications. The imaging descriptors are already available, and the question is which profile is typically benign.
question.breast-imaging.calcification.se.stem: Which calcification profile is categorized as typically benign?

answerChoices.label: Coarse, large, densely calcified, confluent calcifications
Fine pleomorphic calcifications
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Fine pleomorphic calcifications are a suspicious morphology.

answerChoices.label: Fine linear-branching calcifications
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Fine linear or fine linear-branching calcifications are a suspicious morphology.

answerChoices.label: Coarse heterogeneous calcifications
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Coarse heterogeneous calcifications are in the suspicious lexicon rather than the typically benign group.

question.breast-imaging.calcification.se.explanation: The coarse densely calcified pattern is typically benign. The other listed morphologies are in the suspicious lexicon.

question.breast-imaging.calcification.di.patientPresentation: A patient presents with diagnostic mammography results describing calcification morphology and distribution. No biopsy result is available.
question.breast-imaging.calcification.di.stem: Which statement about a segmental distribution of breast calcifications is most accurate?

answerChoices.label: It is a distribution descriptor that must be interpreted with calcification morphology and the complete imaging assessment; it does not by itself diagnose cancer
Segmental distribution automatically confirms breast cancer
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Distribution alone does not provide tissue diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Calcification distribution has no role in imaging assessment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Distribution is an imaging descriptor that contributes to the complete assessment.

answerChoices.label: Every diffuse calcification pattern requires tissue diagnosis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The complete morphology and imaging assessment determine whether tissue diagnosis is indicated.

question.breast-imaging.calcification.di.explanation: Distribution modifies interpretation but does not replace morphology, the rest of the examination, or tissue diagnosis when indicated.

question.breast-mass.age-30-to-39.initia.patientPresentation: A nonpregnant, nonlactating 34-year-old woman at average breast-cancer risk presents with a new persistent palpable breast mass and no overt inflammatory findings.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: MRI is not the appropriate sole initial imaging plan for this scoped presentation.

answerChoices.label: Observe without imaging unless the mass enlarges
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A new persistent palpable mass in this age group warrants diagnostic imaging.

question.breast-mass.age-30-to-39.initia.explanation: For this scoped patient age 30 to 39 with a new palpable mass, diagnostic mammography or tomosynthesis and targeted ultrasound are appropriate components of the initial imaging evaluation.

question.breast-mass.age-30-to-39.initia.patientPresentation: A nonpregnant, nonlactating 38-year-old woman at average breast-cancer risk presents with a newly noticed discrete breast mass without erythema, drainage, or other overt inflammatory findings.

Wait for the next annual screening mammogram

answerChoices.label: Order PET/CT as the initial breast imaging study
answerChoices.distractorRationale: PET/CT is not the appropriate initial breast imaging approach for this scoped presentation.

answerChoices.label: Proceed directly to surgical excision before diagnostic imaging
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The approved pathway begins with diagnostic imaging rather than cancer-directed surgery without imaging or tissue diagnosis.

question.breast-mass.age-30-to-39.initia.explanation: For this scoped patient age 30 to 39, diagnostic mammography or tomosynthesis and targeted ultrasound are appropriate initial imaging modalities. Subsequent tissue diagnosis depends on the complete assessment.

question.postoperative-ascites.cross-sec.patientPresentation: A patient recently underwent extensive abdominal surgery at another center. They present to the surgical clinic with progressive abdominal swelling, diffuse discomfort, and early satiety. They are hemodynamically stable without peritonitis.
question.postoperative-ascites.cross-sec.stem: Which initial imaging study is most appropriate for this stable postoperative presentation?

answerChoices.label: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
Abdominal radiographs
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Radiographs do not adequately characterize the extent of intraperitoneal fluid or broadly evaluate the postoperative abdomen in this presentation.

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This targeted study does not provide the broad initial evaluation needed when the cause of progressive postoperative abdominal swelling is not yet established.

answerChoices.label: Upper gastrointestinal contrast series
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This does not provide the broad cross-sectional evaluation needed for the approved nonlocalized postoperative presentation.

question.postoperative-ascites.cross-sec.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT evaluates the distribution of fluid and other postoperative complications. In this pathway it shows large-volume intraperitoneal fluid without obstruction, hemorrhage, or a discrete abscess, but it does not establish the fluid's composition.

question.chylous-ascites.fluid-confirmat.patientPresentation: CT demonstrates large-volume intraperitoneal fluid without obstruction, hemorrhage, or a discrete abscess. The patient remains stable, but the fluid's cause has not been established.
question.chylous-ascites.fluid-confirmat.stem: What is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of the ascites?

answerChoices.label: Image-guided diagnostic paracentesis with fluid triglycerides and studies for infection and other plausible postoperative leaks
Diagnose chylous ascites from the CT appearance alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CT establishes the presence and extent of ascites but cannot confirm that its composition is chylous.

answerChoices.label: Proceed directly to lymphangiography without sampling the fluid
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Fluid confirmation comes before invasive lymphatic localization in this stable initial pathway.

answerChoices.label: Repeat CT after a period of unrestricted diet
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeat anatomic imaging does not establish the fluid's composition and delays diagnostic sampling.

question.chylous-ascites.fluid-confirmat.explanation: Diagnostic sampling identifies the fluid and evaluates competing postoperative causes. In this pathway, paracentesis yields milky fluid with elevated triglycerides and no evidence of infection, bile leak, or pancreatic leak, confirming postoperative chylous ascites.

question.postoperative-chylous-ascites.i.patientPresentation: Diagnostic paracentesis confirms postoperative chylous ascites. The ascites is large, symptomatic, and reaccumulates after diagnostic sampling.
question.postoperative-chylous-ascites.i.stem: What is the most appropriate initial treatment plan?

answerChoices.label: Admit for symptom-directed peritoneal drainage, a low-long-chain-triglyceride diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides, and nutritional, fluid, and electrolyte monitoring
Discharge with an unrestricted diet and no nutritional or fluid monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Large symptomatic reaccumulating chylous ascites requires active management and monitoring rather than unrestricted outpatient observation.

answerChoices.label: Proceed immediately to lymphangiography and embolization before conservative treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Invasive lymphatic localization and intervention are generally reserved for selected persistent or severe refractory cases rather than used before initial conservative management in this stable presentation.

answerChoices.label: Proceed immediately to operative lymphatic ligation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Immediate reoperation is not the preferred first treatment for this stable patient before an initial conservative hospital-management trial.

question.postoperative-chylous-ascites.i.explanation: For this large symptomatic reaccumulating postoperative leak, initial care combines drainage when needed for symptoms and accumulation, a low-long-chain-triglyceride diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides, and close nutritional and fluid monitoring. Invasive localization or repair is reserved for an individualized persistent or refractory course.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.vitamin.patientPresentation: A patient recovering after an outpatient procedure asks which vitamin directly supports collagen formation during healing.
question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.vitamin.stem: Which vitamin serves as a cofactor for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen biosynthesis?

answerChoices.label: Vitamin A
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vitamin A has other roles in epithelial biology and wound healing but is not the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases.

answerChoices.label: Vitamin D
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vitamin D primarily regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis rather than this collagen-hydroxylation step.

answerChoices.label: Vitamin K
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vitamin K supports gamma-carboxylation of selected proteins and is not the cofactor for proline and lysine hydroxylation in collagen.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.vitamin.explanation: Vitamin C supports prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase activity during collagen biosynthesis. This is a general collagen-maturation mechanism, not a type III-only effect.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.biochem.patientPresentation: While monitoring a patient in the Peri-op/Recovery Room, the team reviews why severe vitamin C deficiency can weaken healing tissue.
question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.biochem.stem: Which step in collagen synthesis depends directly on vitamin C?

answerChoices.label: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen
Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a vitamin K-dependent process rather than the vitamin C-dependent collagen step.

answerChoices.label: Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reaction depends on vitamin B12 and is not the collagen-hydroxylation step.

answerChoices.label: Increased intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is associated with vitamin D signaling rather than collagen hydroxylation.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.biochem.explanation: Ascorbate is required for hydroxylation of selected proline and lysine residues during procollagen maturation.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.mechani.patientPresentation: A postoperative patient asks what ascorbate actually does during collagen formation.

answerChoices.label: It supports the activity of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases needed for collagen maturation and stability
It becomes a structural amino acid within collagen
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vitamin C is a cofactor; it is not incorporated into collagen as a structural amino acid.

answerChoices.label: It converts type I collagen into type III collagen
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Collagen types are not produced by vitamin C converting one mature type into another.

answerChoices.label: It activates vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation, not vitamin C, supports activation of those clotting proteins.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.mechani.explanation: Vitamin C supports the hydroxylase enzymes required for normal collagen maturation and stability; it is neither a collagen amino acid nor a collagen-type converter.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.mechani.patientPresentation: A patient with markedly limited dietary variety has impaired wound healing, prompting a review of collagen biochemistry.
question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.mechani.stem: Which consequence most directly follows from inadequate vitamin C availability during collagen synthesis?

answerChoices.label: Impaired proline and lysine hydroxylation, producing less stable collagen
Selective loss of type III collagen with normal type I collagen
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation mechanism is not limited to type III collagen.

answerChoices.label: Excessive gamma-carboxylation of coagulation proteins
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gamma-carboxylation is a vitamin K-dependent pathway and is not increased by vitamin C inadequacy.

answerChoices.label: Reduced intestinal calcium absorption causing immediate scar mineralization
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This combines an unrelated vitamin D mechanism with a consequence not produced by vitamin C-dependent collagen hydroxylation.

question.wound-healing.vitamin-c.mechani.explanation: Inadequate ascorbate impairs proline and lysine hydroxylation, compromising normal collagen maturation and stability and thereby contributing to impaired healing.

question.gastric-malt.integrated-patholo.patientPresentation: An adult with persistent dyspepsia undergoes EGD. Gastric biopsies show a dense infiltrate of small lymphocytes expanding the lamina propria and infiltrating glands. The cells are CD20 and CD79a positive, with CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1 absent; no sheets of large cells are present.
question.gastric-malt.integrated-patholo.stem: Which diagnosis best fits the integrated biopsy findings?

answerChoices.label: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the stomach
answerChoices.distractorRationale: DLBCL is characterized by sheets of transformed large B cells, which are absent in this approved presentation.

answerChoices.label: Gastric adenocarcinoma with reactive lymphoid inflammation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The biopsy describes a clonal-appearing small B-cell process with lymphoepithelial lesions rather than malignant epithelial cells.

answerChoices.label: Mantle cell lymphoma involving the gastric mucosa
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Mantle cell lymphoma commonly expresses CD5 and cyclin D1, unlike the approved immunophenotype.

question.gastric-malt.integrated-patholo.explanation: Small B cells infiltrating gastric glands to form lymphoepithelial lesions, with CD20 and CD79a expression and absent CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1, support gastric MALT lymphoma. The morphology and immunophenotype must be interpreted together.

question.gastric-malt.pathology-profile-.patientPresentation: An adult with epigastric discomfort has an abnormal gastric biopsy after EGD. The pathologist is comparing the morphology and immunophenotype with common gastric malignancies.
question.gastric-malt.pathology-profile-.stem: Which pathologic profile most strongly supports gastric MALT lymphoma?

answerChoices.label: Small CD20-positive B cells forming lymphoepithelial lesions; CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1 absent
Sheets of large CD20-positive cells with brisk proliferation, destructive growth, and no dominant small-cell infiltrate
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This profile supports an aggressive large B-cell lymphoma rather than classic low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma.

answerChoices.label: Cytokeratin-positive signet-ring cells infiltrating the gastric wall with a prominent desmoplastic stromal response
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is an epithelial gastric malignancy rather than a small B-cell lymphoma.

answerChoices.label: Small CD5- and cyclin D1-positive B cells expanding the mucosa in a pattern compatible with mantle cell lymphoma
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CD5 and cyclin D1 positivity favors mantle cell lymphoma, not the usual gastric MALT phenotype.

question.gastric-malt.pathology-profile-.explanation: The combination of small B-cell morphology, lymphoepithelial lesions, and a CD20-positive, CD5-negative, CD10-negative, cyclin D1-negative phenotype supports gastric MALT lymphoma.

question.gastric-malt.cd20-alone-boundar.patientPresentation: A limited gastric biopsy from an adult with dyspepsia contains many CD20-positive lymphocytes, but the specimen lacks convincing lymphoepithelial lesions and other diagnostic morphology.
question.gastric-malt.cd20-alone-boundar.stem: How should the CD20 result be interpreted?

answerChoices.label: CD20 confirms B-cell lineage, not MALT lymphoma by itself
CD20 alone confirms gastric MALT lymphoma even without diagnostic morphology
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CD20 identifies B cells but is not specific for MALT lymphoma and cannot replace integrated morphologic assessment.

answerChoices.label: CD20 positivity proves diffuse large B-cell lymphoma regardless of cell size
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Large-cell morphology and other pathologic features are required to diagnose DLBCL.

answerChoices.label: CD20 positivity proves the infiltrate is reactive and excludes lymphoma
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Both reactive and neoplastic B cells may express CD20, so this conclusion is unsupported.

question.gastric-malt.cd20-alone-boundar.explanation: CD20 establishes that the infiltrate contains B cells. It does not distinguish reactive B cells from gastric MALT lymphoma without compatible morphology, immunophenotyping, and any additional evaluation needed for an equivocal biopsy.

question.gastric-malt.localized-hpylori-.patientPresentation: An adult has confirmed localized low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma. H. pylori testing is positive, staging shows no disseminated disease, and the biopsy has no large-cell transformation.
question.gastric-malt.localized-hpylori-.stem: What is the most appropriate initial lymphoma-directed plan?

answerChoices.label: H. pylori eradication therapy, then response reassessment
Immediate gastrectomy followed by routine postoperative surveillance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gastrectomy is not the preferred initial treatment for this classic localized low-grade eradication-responsive presentation.

answerChoices.label: Immediate R-CHOP before attempting H. pylori eradication therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Aggressive systemic lymphoma treatment is not the initial approach for this low-grade nontransformed presentation.

answerChoices.label: Definitive gastric radiotherapy without an initial eradication attempt
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The approved classic H. pylori-positive localized presentation should first receive eradication therapy.

question.gastric-malt.localized-hpylori-.explanation: H. pylori eradication is initial lymphoma-directed treatment for this classic localized low-grade presentation. Eradication must be confirmed and lymphoma response reassessed; this is not permission to omit follow-up.

question.gastric-malt.eradication-patien.patientPresentation: The endoscopy team is reviewing newly diagnosed gastric lymphoma cases and deciding which patient fits an eradication-first pathway.
question.gastric-malt.eradication-patien.stem: Which patient best fits initial treatment with H. pylori eradication?

answerChoices.label: Localized H. pylori-positive low-grade gastric MALT without transformation
Gastric diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with sheets of transformed large cells
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is an aggressive transformed histology and does not fit the approved classic low-grade eradication-first concept.

answerChoices.label: Localized gastric MALT that progressed after confirmed H. pylori eradication
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Progression after an adequate eradication pathway requires reassessment and a different treatment decision.

answerChoices.label: Disseminated symptomatic gastric MALT with threatened organ function
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Threatening or advanced symptomatic disease requires specialist reassessment rather than an eradication-only strategy.

question.gastric-malt.eradication-patien.explanation: The approved eradication-first teaching point applies to localized low-grade H. pylori-positive gastric MALT without transformation or threatening disease.

question.gastric-malt.eradication-respon.patientPresentation: An adult with localized H. pylori-positive low-grade gastric MALT is preparing to begin eradication therapy and asks what happens after the medication course.
question.gastric-malt.eradication-respon.stem: Which explanation best describes the treatment pathway?

answerChoices.label: Eradicate H. pylori first, then reassess the lymphoma response
Because CD20 is positive, begin rituximab before addressing H. pylori
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CD20 expression does not displace eradication as the initial strategy for this approved presentation.

answerChoices.label: Any CD20-positive gastric lymphoma can be treated with eradication alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CD20 is not disease-specific, and aggressive or nonclassic gastric lymphomas require different management.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy is required before response can be assessed endoscopically
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Endoscopic biopsy reassessment follows eradication; routine gastrectomy is not required for this pathway.

question.gastric-malt.eradication-respon.explanation: Eradication is the initial lymphoma treatment, not the end of care. Confirm eradication and reassess the gastric lymphoma endoscopically and histologically, recognizing that regression may be delayed.

question.gastroparesis.general-confirmat.patientPresentation: An adult has persistent nausea, early satiety, postprandial fullness, and episodic vomiting. Upper endoscopy shows no mechanical gastric-outlet obstruction.
question.gastroparesis.general-confirmat.stem: Which test best documents suspected gastroparesis?

answerChoices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry with impedance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Esophageal manometry evaluates esophageal pressure and coordination rather than measuring solid-meal gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Repeat upper endoscopy with systematic gastric biopsies
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Upper endoscopy can evaluate mucosal disease and obstruction but does not quantify gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Twenty-four-hour ambulatory esophageal pH monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Ambulatory pH monitoring evaluates esophageal acid exposure rather than delayed gastric emptying.

question.gastroparesis.general-confirmat.explanation: Compatible symptoms and exclusion of mechanical obstruction establish suspicion, but delayed gastric emptying must be documented objectively. Four-hour solid-meal scintigraphy measures that emptying.

question.gastroparesis.diabetes-confirma.patientPresentation: An adult with diabetes has chronic nausea, early satiety, postprandial fullness, and vomiting. Imaging has excluded mechanical obstruction.
question.gastroparesis.diabetes-confirma.stem: Which study should be used to confirm delayed gastric emptying?

answerChoices.label: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study with small-bowel follow-through
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A contrast study may evaluate anatomy and transit patterns but is not the approved standardized test for documenting solid-meal gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Prolonged ambulatory reflux monitoring off acid suppression
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reflux monitoring measures esophageal reflux exposure and does not confirm delayed gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Four-hour scintigraphy after a standardized solid meal
High-resolution esophageal manometry with impedance monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Esophageal manometry evaluates esophageal motor function rather than gastric emptying.

question.gastroparesis.diabetes-confirma.explanation: Once mechanical obstruction has been excluded, a four-hour standardized solid-meal scintigraphic study provides objective evidence of delayed gastric emptying.

question.gastroparesis.postsurgical-conf.patientPresentation: After foregut surgery, an adult develops chronic early satiety, nausea, and postprandial fullness. Endoscopy excludes a fixed obstruction.
question.gastroparesis.postsurgical-conf.stem: What is the best confirmatory study?

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopy after an overnight fast with gastric biopsies
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeat endoscopy can reassess anatomy and mucosa but does not objectively quantify the rate of gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry with impedance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Esophageal manometry characterizes esophageal motor function rather than solid-meal gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Twenty-four-hour ambulatory pH monitoring off therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Ambulatory pH monitoring evaluates reflux burden and does not supply the required gastric-emptying measurement.

question.gastroparesis.postsurgical-conf.explanation: Prior surgery can be part of the clinical context, but confirmation still requires objective delayed gastric emptying after obstruction is excluded. Four-hour solid-meal scintigraphy provides that measurement.

question.gastroparesis.objective-result-.patientPresentation: An adult has compatible upper gastrointestinal symptoms, and mechanical obstruction has been excluded. Several test results are available.
question.gastroparesis.objective-result-.stem: Which result supplies the objective motility evidence needed to diagnose gastroparesis?

answerChoices.label: Normal mucosa on repeat upper endoscopy with routine biopsies
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A normal endoscopy may help exclude structural or mucosal disease but does not document delayed gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Delayed solid-meal emptying on four-hour scintigraphy
Abnormal distal acid exposure on ambulatory pH monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Abnormal acid exposure supports reflux physiology, not objective delay in gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Normal esophageal peristalsis on high-resolution manometry
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Normal esophageal peristalsis does not establish delayed gastric emptying.

question.gastroparesis.objective-result-.explanation: Gastroparesis requires objective evidence of delayed gastric emptying after obstruction has been excluded. Delayed solid-meal emptying on four-hour scintigraphy supplies that evidence.

question.postoperative-ileus.prolonged-d.patientPresentation: An adult is eight days removed from major abdominal surgery. Severe ileus and high nasogastric output persist. Mechanical obstruction has been excluded, reversible contributors have been addressed, and oral or enteral nutrition remains infeasible.
question.postoperative-ileus.prolonged-d.stem: What nutritional support should be initiated?

answerChoices.label: Continue maintenance IV fluids alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Maintenance fluid does not provide adequate nutritional support for this prolonged period of gastrointestinal dysfunction.

answerChoices.label: Begin full-rate gastric tube feeding
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The approved presentation explicitly establishes that enteral feeding remains infeasible and intolerable.

answerChoices.label: Return to the operating room for ileus alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Duration alone is not an indication for reoperation after mechanical obstruction and other operative pathology have been excluded.

question.postoperative-ileus.prolonged-d.explanation: Persistent severe postoperative ileus can prevent adequate oral or enteral nutrition. In this approved presentation, parenteral nutrition supplies nutritional support while the gastrointestinal route remains unusable.

question.postoperative-ileus.prolonged-m.patientPresentation: On postoperative day nine, an adult still has severe ileus with high nasogastric output. Evaluation shows no mechanical obstruction, reversible contributors have been addressed, and enteral feeding remains intolerable.
question.postoperative-ileus.prolonged-m.stem: Which management addition is most appropriate?

answerChoices.label: Give neostigmine as routine ileus treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Neostigmine is not routine treatment for prolonged postoperative ileus in this approved presentation.

answerChoices.label: Continue NPO without nutritional support
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Continuing prolonged starvation without nutrition support is not appropriate when enteral feeding remains infeasible.

answerChoices.label: Start erythromycin as definitive therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Erythromycin is not definitive treatment for this prolonged postoperative ileus and does not address the established nutritional deficit.

question.postoperative-ileus.prolonged-m.explanation: Because adequate oral and enteral nutrition remain infeasible beyond seven postoperative days, parenteral nutrition should be added as nutritional support. It does not replace continued supportive ileus care.

question.postoperative-ileus.parenteral-.patientPresentation: The inpatient surgical service is deciding which postoperative patient most clearly needs parenteral nutritional support.
question.postoperative-ileus.parenteral-.stem: Which postoperative patient most clearly warrants parenteral nutrition?

answerChoices.label: POD 2 with mild distention while oral liquids meet nutritional needs
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This patient is tolerating adequate oral intake and does not meet the approved indication.

answerChoices.label: POD 4 with ileus while enteral feeding safely meets nutritional needs
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Parenteral nutrition is not indicated by the ileus label alone when enteral nutrition is safely adequate.

answerChoices.label: POD 8 with severe ileus, no obstruction, and enteral feeding infeasible
POD 8 with high NG output while obstruction remains incompletely evaluated
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Mechanical obstruction and other precipitating pathology must be evaluated rather than assuming prolonged postoperative ileus from the day and tube output alone.

question.postoperative-ileus.parenteral-.explanation: The approved indication requires prolonged severe ileus, exclusion of mechanical obstruction, and inability to provide adequate oral or enteral nutrition. The postoperative day or nasogastric output alone is insufficient.

question.postoperative-ileus.parenteral-.patientPresentation: Parenteral nutrition is started for a patient with prolonged severe postoperative ileus who cannot tolerate enteral feeding.
question.postoperative-ileus.parenteral-.stem: What is its role in this situation?

answerChoices.label: Provide nutrition while enteral feeding remains infeasible
Directly restore bowel motility and terminate the ileus
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Parenteral nutrition supports nutritional needs but does not directly reverse postoperative bowel dysmotility.

answerChoices.label: Replace further evaluation for postoperative mechanical obstruction
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Nutritional support never replaces evaluation for obstruction or another treatable postoperative diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Prevent any future transition back to enteral nutrition
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Oral or enteral nutrition should resume when gastrointestinal function and tolerance permit.

question.postoperative-ileus.parenteral-.explanation: Parenteral nutrition supplies nutrients while the gastrointestinal route is unusable. It does not treat the ileus itself, replace diagnostic reassessment, or prevent a later transition back to oral or enteral feeding.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.post-end.patientPresentation: A patient has resectable proximal gastric adenocarcinoma. Staging shows no greater-curvature extension, splenic invasion, or suspicious splenic-hilar nodes. Curative gastrectomy is planned.
question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.post-end.stem: What should the operative referral recommend regarding the spleen?

answerChoices.label: Add splenectomy to every total gastrectomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A planned total gastrectomy is not by itself an indication for prophylactic splenectomy.

answerChoices.label: Add splenectomy for proximal location alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Proximal location alone does not justify routine splenic removal in the approved population.

answerChoices.label: Add splenectomy solely to increase node yield
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Increasing node yield alone does not provide a survival justification for prophylactic splenectomy.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.post-end.explanation: In proximal gastric adenocarcinoma without greater-curvature invasion, direct splenic invasion, or suspected splenic-hilar disease, routine prophylactic splenectomy adds morbidity without improving survival.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.patientPresentation: A patient asks why the surgeon plans to preserve the spleen during curative resection of a proximal gastric cancer that does not involve the greater curvature or spleen and has no suspected splenic-hilar disease.

answerChoices.label: Spleen preservation maintains survival with less morbidity
Routine splenectomy improves survival despite added operative morbidity
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The randomized and guideline evidence does not show a survival advantage from routine prophylactic splenectomy.

answerChoices.label: Splenectomy is required for every curative resection
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Curative intent does not make prophylactic splenectomy routinely necessary in this defined population.

answerChoices.label: Proximal location alone mandates splenic removal
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The relevant boundaries are greater-curvature, splenic, and splenic-hilar involvement rather than proximal location alone.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.explanation: Spleen preservation maintains oncologic survival and avoids the additional morbidity of prophylactic splenectomy in the approved operative population.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.patientPresentation: The hospital surgical team is reviewing several patients with proximal gastric adenocarcinoma before definitive operative planning.
question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.stem: Which patient most clearly fits the evidence supporting routine spleen preservation?

answerChoices.label: Proximal cancer without greater-curvature, splenic, or hilar involvement
Proximal cancer with direct tumor invasion extending into splenic parenchyma
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Direct splenic invasion falls outside the routine prophylactic-splenectomy evidence addressed by this concept.

answerChoices.label: Proximal cancer with suspected metastatic disease in splenic-hilar nodes
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Suspected splenic-hilar disease falls outside the narrowly approved routine spleen-preservation population.

answerChoices.label: Proximal cancer with extensive tumor invasion along the greater curvature
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Greater-curvature invasion was excluded from the pivotal routine-prophylaxis population and requires separate operative planning.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.explanation: The strongest routine spleen-preservation evidence applies when proximal gastric cancer does not involve the greater curvature, spleen, or splenic-hilar nodes.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.patientPresentation: A patient with resectable proximal gastric adenocarcinoma otherwise meets the criteria for spleen-preserving gastrectomy.
question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.stem: Which new finding makes the routine spleen-preservation rule less directly applicable?

answerChoices.label: Direct extension of the tumor into the spleen
Location of the tumor in the proximal stomach
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Proximal location is part of the approved scenario and does not alone justify splenectomy.

answerChoices.label: A planned total gastrectomy for oncologic resection
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Total gastrectomy alone does not make prophylactic splenectomy beneficial.

answerChoices.label: Need for standard regional lymph-node staging
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Standard regional nodal staging does not by itself require removal of the spleen.

question.gastric-adenocarcinoma.spleen-p.explanation: Direct splenic invasion is outside the routine prophylactic setting. This boundary does not independently prescribe an operation; it signals that individualized oncologic planning is required.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.patientPresentation: Eight hours after an extensive burn, a patient is stable following resuscitation. The gastrointestinal tract is functional, no enteral contraindication exists, and oral intake cannot meet nutritional needs.

answerChoices.label: Continue IV fluids without nutrition for 48 hours
answerChoices.distractorRationale: IV fluid resuscitation does not replace nutritional support, and an unnecessary delay forfeits the early-enteral window.

answerChoices.label: Start parenteral nutrition before attempting enteral feeding
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Routine first-line parenteral nutrition is not preferred when the gastrointestinal tract is usable.

answerChoices.label: Wait until all grafting procedures are complete
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Planned grafting does not justify postponing otherwise feasible early enteral nutrition.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.explanation: This stable, adequately resuscitated patient has no enteral contraindication and cannot meet nutritional needs orally, so enteral tube feeding should begin now. Eight hours is the presentation context, not a universal cutoff; the canonical rule is as soon as feasible within 24 hours.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.patientPresentation: A patient with extensive burns has been adequately resuscitated and has no contraindication to enteral nutrition.

answerChoices.label: As soon as feasible within the first 24 hours
Only after bowel sounds have returned
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Waiting for bowel sounds creates an unnecessary delay when the patient is otherwise ready and has no enteral contraindication.

answerChoices.label: After 48 hours of observation without nutrition
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A routine 48-hour delay conflicts with the approved early-enteral strategy.

answerChoices.label: Once all planned operations have been completed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Completion of every planned operation is not a prerequisite for starting otherwise feasible enteral nutrition.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.explanation: For an adequately resuscitated patient with an extensive burn and no enteral contraindication, begin enteral nutrition as soon as feasible within the first 24 hours.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.patientPresentation: A stable patient with extensive burns cannot meet nutritional needs orally, but the gastrointestinal tract remains usable.
question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.stem: Which nutritional route is preferred initially?

answerChoices.label: Use enteral nutrition while the GI tract is functional
Use parenteral nutrition as routine first-line support
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Parenteral nutrition is not routine first-line support when enteral nutrition is feasible.

answerChoices.label: Provide maintenance crystalloid as sole nutritional therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Maintenance crystalloid does not provide the nutritional support required after an extensive burn.

answerChoices.label: Delay nutrition until spontaneous oral intake is sufficient
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Waiting for adequate spontaneous intake unnecessarily delays nutritional support in this patient.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.explanation: When the gastrointestinal tract is usable, enteral nutrition is the preferred initial route. This concept does not define the feeding-access site, formula, or advancement protocol.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.patientPresentation: The burn ICU team is deciding which patient most clearly fits the approved early-enteral-nutrition pathway.
question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.stem: Which patient most clearly fits this early-enteral-nutrition concept?

answerChoices.label: Extensive burn, adequately resuscitated, with no enteral contraindication
Extensive burn with ongoing shock and incomplete hemodynamic resuscitation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Ongoing shock and incomplete resuscitation place the patient outside the approved early-feeding scenario.

answerChoices.label: Extensive burn with suspected intestinal ischemia or mechanical obstruction
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Suspected ischemia or obstruction is an enteral safety concern and falls outside this teaching pathway.

answerChoices.label: Limited burn with nutritional needs already met through ordinary oral intake
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This patient does not require enteral tube feeding to meet nutritional needs.

question.severe-burn.early-enteral-nutri.explanation: The concept applies to an extensively burned patient who is adequately resuscitated, cannot meet nutritional needs orally, and has no enteral contraindication. The other patients either do not need tube feeding or require a different safety pathway.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.patientPresentation: During elective ventral hernia repair, a small-bowel enterotomy is recognized and securely repaired. Contamination is minimal and controlled, there is no ongoing gross spillage, and the stable patient remains appropriate for single-stage repair.

answerChoices.label: Biologic mesh solely because an enterotomy occurred
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A controlled enterotomy does not by itself make biologic mesh the preferred material.

answerChoices.label: Permanent microporous multifilament synthetic mesh in the controlled field
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The approved material profile is macroporous and monofilament rather than microporous and multifilament.

answerChoices.label: Rapidly absorbable mesh as the routine choice for every contaminated field
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Clean-contaminated status does not make rapidly absorbable mesh the routine default for the selected repair.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.explanation: Once secure enterotomy repair, source control, minimal contamination, absence of gross spillage, and appropriateness of single-stage repair are established, select permanent macroporous monofilament synthetic mesh. This is a narrow material-selection rule, not permission to proceed after every enterotomy.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.patientPresentation: A stable patient is proceeding with single-stage incisional hernia repair after a recognized enterotomy was securely repaired with source control and no gross enteric spillage. The team is comparing mesh construction.

answerChoices.label: Permanent, multifilament, and microporous
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Microporous multifilament construction is not the preferred profile for this approved scenario.

answerChoices.label: Biologic and selected solely because of contamination
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Contamination alone does not establish biologic mesh as superior to permanent synthetic mesh.

answerChoices.label: Rapidly absorbable regardless of source control
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Source control and operative context cannot be bypassed by selecting an absorbable material.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.explanation: Permanent macroporous monofilament synthetic mesh is the approved material profile for this selected, controlled single-stage repair.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.patientPresentation: The hospital hernia team is reviewing operative cases in which a bowel injury or contamination was encountered during ventral or incisional hernia repair.
question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.stem: Which patient most clearly fits the approved macroporous-synthetic-mesh selection rule?

answerChoices.label: Stable patient with a repaired enterotomy, source control, and no gross spillage
Unstable patient with ongoing enteric contamination and no completed source control
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Instability and incomplete source control place the patient outside the approved selection rule.

answerChoices.label: Ischemic bowel perforation with uncontrolled feculent spillage throughout the field
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Uncontrolled feculent contamination is outside the narrowly approved controlled-enterotomy scenario.

answerChoices.label: Uncertain bowel viability with incomplete source control and persistent contamination
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Uncertain viability and persistent contamination require individualized management beyond this concept.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.explanation: The approved rule applies only to a stable patient after secure repair and source control with minimal controlled contamination and no gross spillage, once single-stage repair has already been selected.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.patientPresentation: A recognized small-bowel enterotomy occurs during elective incisional hernia repair. The operative team is assessing whether the narrow controlled-enterotomy mesh-selection rule remains applicable.
question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.stem: Which finding most clearly takes the case outside the approved rule?

answerChoices.label: Persistent gross enteric spillage despite attempted source control
Secure primary repair of the recognized enterotomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Secure repair is one of the prerequisites for the approved controlled-enterotomy scenario.

answerChoices.label: Minimal contamination controlled intraoperatively
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Minimal controlled contamination is within the approved scenario rather than an exclusion.

answerChoices.label: Stable physiology after the recognized bowel injury is securely repaired and controlled
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Stable physiology following secure repair and control supports, rather than excludes, the narrow scenario.

question.ventral-hernia.controlled-enter.explanation: Persistent gross spillage means source control and minimal-contamination requirements are not met. The finding takes the case outside this mesh-selection rule but does not independently prescribe the alternative operation.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.patientPresentation: After penetrating thoracic trauma, a stable patient has a localized middle thoracic esophageal perforation and an azygos-vein injury requiring operative control. There is no cardiac, great-arterial, distal-esophageal, or dominant left-pleural injury.
question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.stem: Which incision provides the most direct exposure to both injuries?

answerChoices.label: Left posterolateral thoracotomy for distal thoracic exposure
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A left-sided approach favors the distal esophagus and descending thoracic aorta rather than this middle-esophageal and azygos injury pair.

answerChoices.label: Median sternotomy for central anterior mediastinal exposure
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Median sternotomy is useful for central anterior cardiac and great-vessel exposure but is not the most direct route to both specified posterior-right targets.

answerChoices.label: Left anterolateral thoracotomy for immediate resuscitative access
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a stable patient with localized injuries undergoing planned repair, not a patient requiring immediate resuscitative chest access.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.explanation: A planned right posterolateral thoracotomy provides direct access to the middle thoracic esophagus and azygos vein in this stable, anatomically localized scenario. The answer does not make it the default incision for every thoracic-trauma operation.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.patientPresentation: The trauma team is selecting a planned operative exposure after localizing a stable patient's thoracic injuries.
question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.stem: Which injury combination is most directly exposed through a right thoracotomy?

answerChoices.label: Proximal thoracic esophagus and azygos vein
Distal thoracic esophagus and descending thoracic aorta
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Both targets are generally better exposed from the left chest.

answerChoices.label: Heart and ascending aorta in the anterior mediastinum
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Median sternotomy generally provides the most direct planned exposure to these anterior central structures.

answerChoices.label: Cervical esophagus and left carotid sheath
answerChoices.distractorRationale: These cervical structures require a neck exposure rather than a right thoracotomy.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.explanation: The proximal intrathoracic esophagus and azygos vein are both directly accessible from the right chest. This reverse-anatomy formulation tests the same exposure map as the direct incision variants and therefore retains one FSRS concept.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.patientPresentation: A stable patient has localized injuries of the proximal intrathoracic esophagus and intrathoracic trachea below the thoracic inlet. There is no cardiac or great-arterial injury and no need for immediate resuscitative thoracotomy.
question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.stem: Which operative exposure is most appropriate?

answerChoices.label: Left thoracotomy for distal posterior mediastinal exposure
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The specified injuries are proximal and intrathoracic rather than distal left-sided targets.

answerChoices.label: Median sternotomy for anterior cardiac and aortic exposure
answerChoices.distractorRationale: There is no anterior cardiac or great-arterial injury, and sternotomy is not the most direct shared exposure for the two specified structures.

answerChoices.label: Midline laparotomy for transabdominal upper-abdominal access
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A transabdominal approach does not directly expose the proximal intrathoracic esophagus and trachea.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.explanation: A right thoracotomy provides shared exposure to the proximal intrathoracic esophagus and intrathoracic trachea. The exact posterolateral orientation and interspace remain operative-planning details rather than universal facts for every injury.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.patientPresentation: Four trauma patients require thoracic operative planning. The team is deciding whether each patient fits the planned right posterolateral exposure concept.
question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.stem: Which patient is least appropriate for a planned right posterolateral thoracotomy?

answerChoices.label: Traumatic arrest requiring immediate resuscitative chest access
Stable proximal esophageal and azygos injuries requiring planned repair
answerChoices.distractorRationale: These localized right-chest targets fit the planned right thoracotomy exposure concept.

answerChoices.label: Stable localized right superior mediastinal injuries requiring operative control
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Localized right superior mediastinal targets can appropriately favor planned right-sided exposure.

answerChoices.label: Stable middle thoracic esophageal perforation requiring planned primary repair
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A localized middle thoracic esophageal injury in a stable patient fits the planned right-sided exposure rule.

question.thoracic-trauma.right-thoracoto.explanation: Traumatic arrest requiring immediate chest access is a resuscitative situation, generally using an anterior incision that may be extended to a clamshell according to the injury and protocol. It is not the planned posterolateral exposure tested by this concept.

question.meckel-diverticulum.measured-br.patientPresentation: A 22-year-old undergoes laparoscopy for suspected appendicitis. The appendix is normal. A Meckel diverticulum measuring 2 cm long with a 2.5 cm base is inflamed through its base and into the adjacent ileum.

answerChoices.label: Segmental ileal resection including the diverticulum
Simple diverticulectomy at the involved base
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Simple diverticulectomy would leave the adjacent ileal involvement outside the intended resection.

answerChoices.label: Inversion of the diverticulum without resection
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Inversion does not remove the inflamed diverticulum, involved base, or adjacent ileal disease.

answerChoices.label: Appendectomy alone with observation of the diverticulum
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The appendix is normal and the symptomatic Meckel diverticulum requires definitive treatment.

question.meckel-diverticulum.measured-br.explanation: Inflammation involving both the measured broad base and adjacent ileum requires bowel-inclusive resection. The 2.5 cm base supports the morphology but is not, by itself, the reason segmental resection is selected.

question.meckel-diverticulum.narrow-tip-.patientPresentation: A 19-year-old undergoes laparoscopy for right-lower-quadrant pain. The appendix is normal. A Meckel diverticulum is 5 cm long with a 1 cm base. Inflammation is confined to its distal tip; the base and adjacent ileum are healthy.

answerChoices.label: Segmental ileal resection including normal adjacent bowel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The healthy narrow base and normal adjacent ileum do not require segmental bowel resection in this tip-limited scenario.

answerChoices.label: Inversion of the diverticulum without resection
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Inversion does not definitively remove the symptomatic inflamed diverticulum.

answerChoices.label: Appendectomy alone with observation of the diverticulum
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The normal appendix does not explain the operative finding, and the symptomatic Meckel diverticulum should be treated.

question.meckel-diverticulum.narrow-tip-.explanation: A long, narrow diverticulum with tip-limited inflammation and a healthy base and adjacent ileum can be treated with simple diverticulectomy.

question.meckel-diverticulum.reverse-mor.patientPresentation: During abdominal exploration for suspected appendicitis, several patients are found to have symptomatic Meckel diverticula.
question.meckel-diverticulum.reverse-mor.stem: Which operative finding is most suitable for simple diverticulectomy?

answerChoices.label: 5 cm long, 1 cm healthy base, tip-only inflammation
2 cm long, 2.5 cm inflamed base, with adjacent ileal involvement
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The broad involved base and adjacent ileal disease favor bowel-inclusive resection rather than simple diverticulectomy.

answerChoices.label: Perforation at the diverticulum-ileum junction with base inflammation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Perforation and inflammation at the junction make a tip-only simple diverticulectomy inadequate.

answerChoices.label: Inflammation extending through a broad base into the adjacent ileum
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Adjacent ileal extension requires bowel-inclusive treatment rather than removal of the diverticulum alone.

question.meckel-diverticulum.reverse-mor.explanation: Simple diverticulectomy fits a long, narrow diverticulum when inflammation is confined to the tip and the base and adjacent ileum are healthy.

question.meckel-diverticulum.select-segm.patientPresentation: Four patients have symptomatic Meckel diverticula identified during abdominal exploration.
question.meckel-diverticulum.select-segm.stem: Which patient should undergo segmental ileal resection?

answerChoices.label: 2 cm long, 2.5 cm inflamed base, with adjacent ileal involvement
5 cm long, 1 cm healthy base, with inflammation confined to the tip
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Tip-only inflammation with a healthy narrow base is suitable for simple diverticulectomy.

answerChoices.label: 4 cm long, 1 cm viable base, with completely normal adjacent ileum
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The viable narrow base and normal adjacent ileum do not support segmental resection.

answerChoices.label: 6 cm long, 1.5 cm healthy base, with distal inflammation only
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A healthy narrow base with distal-only disease is suitable for diverticulectomy rather than segmental bowel resection.

question.meckel-diverticulum.select-segm.explanation: The patient with an inflamed 2.5 cm base and adjacent ileal involvement requires segmental ileal resection. The exact measurement supports the described morphology, but involvement of the base and ileum makes the answer unambiguous.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.patientPresentation: A hemodynamically stable adult undergoes EGD after recent melena. A duodenal ulcer is no longer actively bleeding but contains a clearly visible vessel.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.stem: What should be done for this endoscopic finding?

answerChoices.label: Give oral PPI without endoscopic treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A nonbleeding visible vessel is a high-risk stigma requiring endoscopic hemostasis rather than medication alone.

answerChoices.label: Biopsy the visible vessel before treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Biopsy does not provide hemostasis and risks disrupting a high-risk vascular stigma.

answerChoices.label: Schedule repeat EGD without treating the vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Deferring treatment leaves the high-risk visible vessel without endoscopic hemostasis.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.explanation: Active spurting, active oozing, and a nonbleeding visible vessel are high-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata that warrant endoscopic hemostasis. A clean base or flat pigmented spot does not require endoscopic treatment solely for that finding.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.select-hi.patientPresentation: During an endoscopy list for adults with recent upper-GI bleeding symptoms, the team compares several peptic-ulcer findings to determine which one requires hemostatic treatment.

answerChoices.label: Ulcer with a nonbleeding visible vessel
Clean-based ulcer without active bleeding
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A clean base is a low-risk stigma that does not require endoscopic hemostasis solely for that finding.

answerChoices.label: Flat pigmented spot without active bleeding
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A flat pigmented spot does not require endoscopic hemostasis solely for that finding.

answerChoices.label: Healed ulcer scar without bleeding stigmata
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A healed scar without a bleeding stigma is not an indication for endoscopic hemostasis.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.select-hi.explanation: Active spurting, active oozing, and a nonbleeding visible vessel are high-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata that warrant endoscopic hemostasis. A clean base or flat pigmented spot does not require endoscopic treatment solely for that finding.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.clean-bas.patientPresentation: A stable adult undergoes EGD after a self-limited episode of dark stool. Several possible ulcer stigmata are being reviewed before an endoscopic treatment decision is made.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.clean-bas.stem: Which finding generally does not require endoscopic hemostasis?

answerChoices.label: Actively spurting ulcer
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Active spurting is a high-risk stigma that requires endoscopic hemostasis.

answerChoices.label: Actively oozing ulcer
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Active oozing is a high-risk stigma that requires endoscopic hemostasis.

answerChoices.label: Ulcer with a nonbleeding visible vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A nonbleeding visible vessel remains a high-risk stigma requiring endoscopic hemostasis.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.clean-bas.explanation: Active spurting, active oozing, and a nonbleeding visible vessel are high-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata that warrant endoscopic hemostasis. A clean base or flat pigmented spot does not require endoscopic treatment solely for that finding.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-oo.patientPresentation: A hospitalized adult with melena has been resuscitated and undergoes EGD. A duodenal ulcer is actively oozing blood.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-oo.stem: What is the appropriate endoscopic response?

answerChoices.label: Observe because the bleeding appears venous
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Active oozing from a peptic ulcer is a treatment indication regardless of this unsupported characterization.

answerChoices.label: Use oral PPI alone and end the procedure
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Medication alone does not replace endoscopic hemostasis for an actively bleeding ulcer.

answerChoices.label: Delay treatment until a second bleeding episode
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The present active bleed is already an indication for endoscopic hemostasis.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-oo.explanation: Active spurting, active oozing, and a nonbleeding visible vessel are high-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata that warrant endoscopic hemostasis. A clean base or flat pigmented spot does not require endoscopic treatment solely for that finding.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.patientPresentation: A stable adult with recent maroon stool undergoes EGD. A gastric ulcer contains a nonbleeding visible vessel, and four possible hemostatic plans are considered.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.stem: Which option is inappropriate as sole endoscopic treatment?

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine plus bipolar coagulation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This pairs epinephrine with a definitive contact-thermal modality and is an acceptable combination pathway.

answerChoices.label: Bipolar coagulation alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Contact thermal therapy is an accepted monotherapy for a nonbleeding visible vessel.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic clip alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Mechanical clip therapy is an accepted monotherapy for a nonbleeding visible vessel.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.explanation: For a nonbleeding visible vessel, accepted thermal or mechanical therapy may be used alone or with epinephrine. Epinephrine alone is not definitive hemostasis, while two definitive modalities are not automatically required.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.patientPresentation: A hemodynamically stable patient undergoing EGD for recent melena has a nonbleeding visible vessel within a peptic ulcer. The endoscopy team is selecting among thermal, injection, and mechanical options.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.stem: Which statement about hemostatic modality selection is correct?

answerChoices.label: Thermal therapy or clipping may be used without epinephrine
Epinephrine alone provides definitive hemostasis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Epinephrine injection alone is not accepted as definitive hemostasis for a high-risk ulcer stigma.

answerChoices.label: Bipolar coagulation must always be combined with clipping
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A nonbleeding visible vessel may receive an accepted thermal modality as monotherapy.

answerChoices.label: An endoscopic clip must always be combined with thermal therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Mechanical clip therapy may be used as monotherapy for a nonbleeding visible vessel.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.visible-v.explanation: For a nonbleeding visible vessel, accepted thermal or mechanical therapy may be used alone or with epinephrine. Epinephrine alone is not definitive hemostasis, while two definitive modalities are not automatically required.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-oo.patientPresentation: A resuscitated hospitalized adult has an actively oozing duodenal ulcer during EGD. Dilute epinephrine is injected and the bleeding slows.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-oo.stem: What should the endoscopist do next?

answerChoices.label: Apply bipolar coagulation to the vessel
End the procedure because the bleeding slowed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Temporary slowing after epinephrine does not provide definitive hemostasis.

answerChoices.label: Inject additional epinephrine and then stop
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Additional epinephrine still leaves the ulcer without a definitive second modality.

answerChoices.label: Observe the vessel without definitive treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Observation does not complete hemostasis after temporary injection control of active bleeding.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-oo.explanation: When the conventional epinephrine pathway is selected for active ulcer bleeding, temporary injection control must be followed by definitive thermal or mechanical hemostasis. This does not make every noninjection monotherapy universally wrong; selected advanced alternatives belong to a separate expert pathway.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-bl.patientPresentation: A resuscitated hospitalized adult has an actively bleeding peptic ulcer at EGD. The endoscopist elects to use the conventional epinephrine-combination pathway with mechanical hemostasis.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-bl.stem: Which complete treatment plan follows that pathway?

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine injection alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Epinephrine alone lacks the definitive mechanical modality specified by the chosen pathway.

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine plus saline injection without definitive hemostasis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A second injection without a definitive thermal or mechanical modality does not complete the pathway.

answerChoices.label: Repeated epinephrine injections without definitive therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating epinephrine does not substitute for definitive mechanical or thermal hemostasis.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-bl.explanation: When the conventional epinephrine pathway is selected for active ulcer bleeding, temporary injection control must be followed by definitive thermal or mechanical hemostasis. This does not make every noninjection monotherapy universally wrong; selected advanced alternatives belong to a separate expert pathway.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-bl.patientPresentation: During hospital EGD for an actively oozing ulcer, the team compares conventional plans that use epinephrine for initial temporary control with plans that provide definitive hemostasis.
question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-bl.stem: Which plan fails to provide a definitive second modality after epinephrine?

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine followed by bipolar coagulation of the identified vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Bipolar coagulation supplies the definitive contact-thermal modality after epinephrine.

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine followed by endoscopic clipping of the identified vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Clipping supplies the definitive mechanical modality after epinephrine.

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine followed only by another epinephrine injection
Bipolar coagulation without injection therapy to definitively treat the vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This uses a definitive thermal modality rather than relying on epinephrine monotherapy; the question does not claim injection is mandatory in every accepted pathway.

question.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.active-bl.explanation: When the conventional epinephrine pathway is selected for active ulcer bleeding, temporary injection control must be followed by definitive thermal or mechanical hemostasis. This does not make every noninjection monotherapy universally wrong; selected advanced alternatives belong to a separate expert pathway.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-next-s.projectPresentation: The surgery center's established method for locating supplies is 'ask Dana.' Dana has requested a quality-improvement project. The team tests a preprocedure supply checklist in one room and reviews the resulting delay data.
question.quality-improvement.pdsa-next-s.stem: What should the team do next?

answerChoices.label: Act on the findings and plan the next PDSA test
Switch QI models and restart without using the findings
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reaching the Act step does not itself require changing frameworks, and discarding the findings defeats the purpose of the test.

answerChoices.label: Perform root cause analysis regardless of what the test showed

answerChoices.label: Discontinue the intervention before interpreting the results
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The team should use the studied results to determine whether to adopt, adapt, or abandon the change.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-next-s.explanation: After a team studies a limited test, it acts on what it learned: adopt and expand cautiously when the result supports the change, adapt and retest when improvement is incomplete, or abandon or redesign an unsuccessful change. question.quality-improvement.pdsa-adapt..projectPresentation: A team introduces color-coded supply bins. Missing-item delays decrease, although several staff members now refer to every bin as 'the gray one.' The improvement does not reach the target.
question.quality-improvement.pdsa-adapt..stem: What is the best next step?

answerChoices.label: Adapt the bins and test the revision in another PDSA cycle
Adopt the unchanged system throughout the entire facility
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Partial improvement without reaching the target supports adaptation and further testing rather than immediate unchanged expansion.

answerChoices.label: Abandon the intervention because the full target was not reached
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A partially successful change can be adapted and tested again rather than discarded solely for missing the full target.

answerChoices.label: Replace PDSA with root cause analysis because improvement was partial
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Partial improvement is a reason to adapt the change and continue linked testing, not an automatic reason to replace the method.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-adapt..explanation: After a team studies a limited test, it acts on what it learned: adopt and expand cautiously when the result supports the change, adapt and retest when improvement is incomplete, or abandon or redesign an unsuccessful change.
